messages.content: I want to design an incremental compiler that soundly reuses cross-module typechecking results even when edits change overload and trait resolution. Across edits, it must match a clean build’s diagnostics and executable behavior, including cases where a newly applicable candidate appears or resolution becomes ambiguous. It also needs to reuse at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. How should I think about those two requirements together?

Correctness and reuse need separate tests. A cached typechecking result is safe only while the facts that justify it still hold. For overload and trait resolution, those facts include more than the candidate ultimately selected: they include the relevant conditions under which other candidates were not selected. Otherwise an edit in another module could introduce a newly applicable candidate while the old result still appears valid.

The 95% requirement is about declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. It does not permit retaining an unsound result to raise the reuse rate, and it is not a claim that 95% of all declarations must be reused after every edit. The challenge is to recognize unchanged dependencies precisely enough that sound invalidation does not turn into unnecessary rechecking.
Why isn’t a dependency on the selected overload or trait candidate enough?

Selection is a conclusion, not the whole basis for that conclusion. A declaration can continue to see exactly the same selected candidate while an edit makes another candidate applicable. A clean build might then select differently or report an ambiguity. If the cached result only records its former selection, it has no reason to reconsider the declaration.

Conceptually, resolution depends on the applicable search space and the rules used to choose within it. A design has to notice relevant changes to that space, including additions and changes that turn an existing candidate from inapplicable to applicable. That is the sense in which dependencies on previously unsuccessful candidates—or on the conditions that excluded them—matter.
Does that mean every edit affecting a possible candidate has to invalidate every use?

Not necessarily. That would be a conservative way to protect correctness, but it could undermine the reuse target. The distinction is whether an edit changes something relevant to a particular declaration’s resolution, not merely whether it touches a module containing some possible candidate.

One way to reason about a prospective design is to ask what semantic information the resolution actually relied on, and whether that information remains equivalent after the edit. If equivalence cannot be established, rechecking is the safe answer. If it can, reuse may be possible. That describes the obligation; it does not prescribe a particular dependency representation.
What does “semantically unchanged” mean here? Is an unchanged file enough?

An unchanged file is not enough for cross-module resolution: a declaration in that file may depend on information changed elsewhere. Conversely, a textual edit elsewhere need not change the resolution facts relevant to that declaration. “Semantically unchanged” is about the dependencies the declaration uses for resolution, not simply whether source text was touched.

The phrase also should not be used to quietly weaken the stated 95% target. That target names declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. A sound design still has to account for any other information needed to justify reusing a typechecking result; the reuse claim and the conditions for safe reuse should be made clear rather than conflated.
Can you walk through the newly applicable candidate case without assuming a particular language’s resolution rules?

Consider a declaration containing a call that a clean build initially resolves to one candidate. Now suppose an edit in another module changes what candidates are available or whether one of them is applicable. The declaration’s own text need not change. On the next build, the clean-build resolution might remain the same, choose something else, or report an ambiguity; the language’s rules determine which.

An incremental compiler cannot infer the answer solely from the fact that the previously selected candidate is unchanged. It must either establish that the edit leaves this call’s resolution dependencies semantically unchanged or reconsider the call. The example illustrates the dependency problem without assuming any particular overload-selection rule.
And trait resolution presents the same kind of risk?

Yes. A cached trait-resolution outcome can depend on which candidates are available and applicable, not just on the candidate recorded as the outcome. An edit outside the declaration may change that picture. The exact circumstances depend on the language, but the correctness question is the same: would a clean build, with the edited inputs, reach the same typechecking conclusion and produce the same diagnostics and executable behavior?

That question has to include a newly applicable candidate and a newly ambiguous resolution, rather than checking only whether an old candidate disappeared.
If the new resolution is ambiguous, what exactly must match the clean build?

The incremental build must match the clean build’s diagnostics for the edited program. It must not silently retain the earlier successful resolution and proceed as if the ambiguity did not exist. More generally, detecting that something changed is not sufficient if the reported diagnostic differs from what clean typechecking would report.

Executable behavior is the other side of the requirement. When the edited program produces an executable, reused typechecking results must not cause it to behave differently from one produced by a clean build. The goal does not trade diagnostic fidelity against runtime fidelity.
Could we measure progress just by counting how many cached declarations were kept?

That count would address only reuse, and even then it needs the right denominator: the stated threshold is at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. Keeping results for declarations with changed dependencies would not demonstrate sound reuse.

Correctness needs an independent comparison against clean builds across edits. In particular, comparisons must be capable of exposing changes in applicable candidates and ambiguities, because those are explicitly part of the requirement. A high cache-hit count cannot establish that the resulting diagnostics or executable behavior match.
So there’s a tension between being conservative and reaching 95%?

Exactly. Broad invalidation can avoid using a stale resolution result, but it can recheck declarations whose resolution dependencies are semantically unchanged. Very narrow invalidation can improve reuse, but it is unsound if it misses a change that affects which overload or trait candidate applies.

The design problem is to make the distinction accurately: reconsider declarations when relevant resolution facts change, while retaining results when those facts remain semantically unchanged and reuse is otherwise justified. The 95% figure makes precision a requirement rather than merely a performance preference.
Is it enough to compare the final selected candidate before and after an edit?

Not by itself. If obtaining the new selection requires redoing the relevant resolution work, that comparison may not provide the intended reuse. More importantly, a final selection alone may not account for diagnostics associated with the resolution process. The required comparison is to clean-build diagnostics and executable behavior, not merely to an identifier for the selected candidate.

As a conceptual soundness test, ask whether every fact needed to justify the cached typechecking result still holds. A matching selected candidate can be part of that evidence, but it is not automatically the whole of it.
How should the 95% target be phrased so it doesn’t hide failures in ambiguity cases?

Keep the two claims explicit. First: after edits, the incremental compiler matches clean-build diagnostics and executable behavior, including newly applicable candidates and ambiguities. Second: it reuses at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged.

An ambiguity caused by changed resolution dependencies cannot be excused as a reuse opportunity; it must be handled like the clean build. Conversely, rechecking large numbers of declarations with semantically unchanged resolution dependencies cannot be called a success merely because the resulting diagnostics are correct. Both conditions have to hold.
What is the central question to ask whenever the compiler wants to reuse a cross-module result?

Ask whether the edited program preserves the semantic facts on which that declaration’s typechecking result depends, particularly the facts governing overload and trait resolution across module boundaries. The check must be sensitive to candidates becoming applicable and to ambiguities, not just to changes in a formerly selected candidate. If the result is reused, the resulting diagnostics and executable behavior must still be those of a clean build. The separate precision question is whether the compiler can establish unchanged resolution dependencies often enough to meet the at-least-95% reuse requirement.

I’d like to make the reuse rule more concrete: cache declaration typechecks against indexed positive and negative resolution queries. After an edit, revalidate affected queries and invalidate only when their semantic outcomes change. How does that address the cross-module problem?

It makes the dependencies of a cached declaration typecheck more explicit. A positive resolution query can represent a resolution fact the typecheck relied on; a negative query can represent a relevant absence or inapplicability that also helped justify the result. Indexing those queries gives the compiler a way to identify which ones an edit might affect, including when the edit is in another module.

The proposed sequence is: identify affected queries, revalidate them under the edited program, and compare their semantic outcomes with the cached ones. If an outcome changes, invalidate declaration typechecks that depend on it. If it does not, that query alone supplies no reason to discard those results. The negative side matters because a newly applicable overload or trait candidate can change resolution without changing the candidate previously recorded as selected.
What’s an example of a negative resolution query? I don’t want “negative” to sound like an error diagnostic.

It need not mean an error. In this proposal, “negative” describes a fact resolution relied on, such as a relevant candidate not being applicable, or a relevant search not finding a candidate that would affect the outcome. A successful typecheck can depend on such a fact: its selected resolution may be justified partly by the absence of an applicable alternative.

The point of caching that negative fact is to revisit it if an edit could make it false. It is a dependency, not necessarily a diagnostic presented to the user.
Suppose the old selected candidate is unchanged, but an edit makes another candidate applicable. Which part catches it?

The affected negative resolution query is the part intended to catch it. The edit could change the answer to a query that previously established that the alternative did not affect resolution. Revalidating that query would reveal a changed semantic outcome, and the dependent declaration typecheck would be invalidated for reconsideration.

This is why caching only a positive record of the selected candidate would be insufficient. The proposal treats relevant non-selection facts as dependencies too, so the unchanged selected candidate is not mistaken for proof that the overall resolution is unchanged.
And if the edit makes the call ambiguous rather than merely giving it a different winner?

That is also a changed semantic outcome. The cached declaration typecheck cannot simply be reused if the resolution facts now lead to ambiguity. Invalidating it allows the edited program to be typechecked and diagnosed as a clean build would.

The comparison must therefore retain enough semantic meaning to distinguish a resolved call from an ambiguous one. Comparing only whether the formerly selected candidate still exists would miss the case you’re asking about.
Why revalidate queries before invalidating declarations? Wouldn’t it be safer just to invalidate everything indexed as affected?

Invalidating everything potentially affected would be conservative, but it would discard typechecking results even when revalidation shows the relevant resolution facts are semantically unchanged. Revalidation separates “an edit could matter to this query” from “the query’s answer actually changed.”

That distinction is central to the reuse objective. The proposal does not claim that an affected query is unchanged simply because the old answer looks plausible; it asks the query again against the edited program. Only an unchanged semantic outcome provides a reason, on this dependency, to retain the cached typecheck.
What work does the index do if we still have to run queries again?

The index is meant to narrow *which* queries need revalidation. An edit may have no bearing on many cached declarations’ resolution queries. Without a way to locate potentially affected queries, the compiler might have to revisit resolution broadly or risk missing a cross-module change.

The index does not itself prove a query’s answer is unchanged. It identifies queries that could be affected; revalidation supplies the semantic comparison. Both parts matter: an index that overlooks a newly applicable candidate would be unsound, while treating every indexed query as changed without checking could sacrifice reuse.
Does “invalidate only changed semantic outcomes” mean the compiler never invalidates a declaration for any other reason?

No. Here, “only” describes the proposed handling of resolution-query dependencies: mere potential impact is not enough to invalidate a cached declaration typecheck if the affected queries revalidate to the same semantic outcomes. It does not assert that resolution is the only possible dependency of typechecking, or exempt a declaration from invalidation if some other required basis for reuse changes.

Likewise, revalidating a resolution query is not the same as declaring the entire cached typecheck reusable. The proposal is specifically about making overload and trait resolution dependencies precise.
I’m still unsure what counts as the query’s “semantic outcome.” Is it just a yes-or-no answer?

Not necessarily. “Semantic outcome” should be read at the level needed to justify the dependent typecheck. A positive or negative query may have an answer richer than a Boolean, and the comparison must not erase a distinction that could change resolution, diagnostics, or executable behavior. For example, an answer that is now ambiguous cannot be treated as equivalent to one that previously resolved successfully.

The proposal states the criterion—compare relevant semantic outcomes—without fixing a particular representation for those outcomes. Choosing an equality notion that is too coarse would undermine soundness; choosing one that treats semantically irrelevant differences as changes would cause avoidable invalidation.
Could the same edit cause some queries to change and others to remain semantically identical?

Yes, that is precisely the distinction the proposal is designed to exploit. The edit can make several indexed queries worth checking without changing every answer. Dependent declaration typechecks are invalidated where the revalidated semantic outcome changes; a query that gives the same semantic answer does not, by itself, force invalidation.

This lets the compiler respond to a genuine resolution change while retaining typechecking results tied to unchanged resolution facts. It is a proposed way to pursue the at-least-95% reuse requirement for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged, not a measured result.
If a candidate wasn’t present before the edit, how could a cached query possibly point to it?

It cannot point to that previously absent candidate as an existing object. The negative query instead has to express a relevant property of the resolution search whose answer could change when a candidate appears or becomes applicable. The index must be able to recognize that an edit could affect that property and schedule its revalidation.

That is a key soundness obligation for this proposal. Recording only dependencies on candidates already encountered would not cover newly applicable candidates. The query and its indexing need to cover relevant changes to the answer, including additions, rather than merely changes to previously named candidates.
Does this proposal dictate how the index represents those searches?

No particular index structure is specified. “Indexed positive and negative resolution queries” says that cached declaration typechecks are associated with resolution queries and that edits can be used to locate queries that may need revalidation. It does not, on its own, settle the representation of a query, the indexing data structure, or the mechanics of revalidation.

Those choices would have to preserve the intended coverage: if an edit can change a query’s semantic outcome, that query must be among those considered. At the same time, sufficiently discriminating indexing helps avoid unnecessary work.
Can I summarize it as: record what resolution found and what relevant searches ruled out, then revisit the affected records after an edit?

That captures the idea, with one useful qualification: revisit the *queries*, not merely the old records as static statements. The edited program may yield a different answer. The compiler uses the index to find queries an edit could affect, revalidates those queries, and invalidates dependent declaration typechecks only where the semantic outcomes have changed.

Including relevant negative queries is what makes the summary cover a candidate that was previously absent or inapplicable. Including the semantic comparison is what prevents every potentially affected declaration from being discarded automatically.
What would make this approach fail the clean-build requirement even if the cache hit rate looked excellent?

A missed affected query would do it: a newly applicable candidate might change resolution, but a cached declaration typecheck would remain in use. A comparison that calls two materially different query outcomes “unchanged” would have a similar effect. Either could conceal a new ambiguity, produce diagnostics that differ from a clean build, or allow executable behavior to differ.

A high reuse rate cannot compensate for that. The proposal’s intended reuse depends on accurately indexing relevant positive and negative queries and correctly recognizing changes in their semantic outcomes.
And what would make it safe but needlessly poor at reuse?

If the index labels many queries as potentially affected, revalidation may cost more work than necessary. More directly, if the compiler invalidates cached declaration typechecks whenever an edit might affect a query—even when revalidation shows its semantic outcome is unchanged—it discards results that this proposal is intended to keep.

The proposed separation between potential impact and actual semantic change addresses that second issue. It does not establish that the 95% threshold has been reached; it gives a way to avoid invalidating declarations solely because an edit touched something near their resolution dependencies.
So what is the proposed rule at the point where a cached declaration typecheck is either kept or discarded?

For the resolution dependencies in this proposal: associate the cached typecheck with indexed positive and negative resolution queries; revalidate queries an edit could affect; and invalidate the dependent typecheck when a relevant query’s semantic outcome changes. An affected query whose semantic outcome remains the same does not, on that ground alone, require invalidation.

The rule is intended to be sensitive to both newly applicable candidates and ambiguities while avoiding needless loss of cross-module typechecking results. Whether a complete compiler satisfies clean-build equivalence and the at-least-95% reuse target still depends on the soundness and precision of those queries, their index, and their outcome comparisons.
How should negative resolution queries represent visibility and applicability so that a new overload or trait implementation invalidates the declarations it affects?

The crucial point is that a negative query cannot mean only “this particular candidate was rejected.” A newly added candidate did not exist when the declaration was cached. The query needs to describe the relevant *search*: what could be visible to this declaration, and what could be applicable to its resolution. After an edit, the compiler must be able to revisit that search even if none of its previously known candidates changed.

It helps to keep visibility and applicability conceptually distinct. A candidate may be inapplicable because it is not visible from the declaration, or it may be visible but fail the conditions for this use. Either situation can change after an edit. The cached negative fact must cover whichever condition mattered to the resolution, without treating every new candidate everywhere as relevant.
Would “no other applicable candidate exists” be a sufficient negative query?

It states the kind of fact that may justify reuse, but it leaves out what “other,” “applicable,” and “exists” mean for this declaration. In particular, the query must be tied to the declaration’s resolution context so an edit that adds a potentially visible candidate can be recognized as affecting it.

A sound representation need not list every candidate that could ever be created. It does need to make the absence claim recheckable: if a new overload or trait implementation could change the answer, the query must be found and revalidated. Otherwise “no other applicable candidate exists” would simply preserve an old conclusion without testing it against the edited program.
How do visibility and applicability interact in that absence claim?

They answer different questions. Visibility asks whether a candidate can participate in resolution from this declaration’s context. Applicability asks whether a participating candidate satisfies the conditions for this particular use. A candidate that fails either may be absent from the applicable set, but those failures are not interchangeable: an edit could change visibility without changing the candidate itself, or change applicability while leaving visibility alone.

The negative query could express the combined result, provided its indexing and revalidation remain sensitive to changes on both sides. Keeping the two ideas distinguishable is useful for checking whether the query really covers all the ways its answer could change; it does not require a particular stored format.
If a new overload is visible but plainly inapplicable, should its addition invalidate the cached declaration?

Its addition may make the negative query worth revalidating. But if revalidation establishes that the relevant semantic outcome has not changed—for example, the new overload still cannot affect this use—then that edit need not invalidate the declaration *on this resolution dependency alone*.

That separates two stages: detecting that an edit could affect a query, and deciding whether the query’s answer actually changed. Invalidating every declaration whose search could see a new overload would be more conservative than the proposed reuse rule.
What if a candidate was already visible, but the edit makes it applicable?

That is why the negative query cannot stop at visibility. If the declaration’s cached result relied on that candidate not being applicable, the edit must cause the relevant query to be reconsidered. If the candidate is now applicable and that changes the resolution outcome, the dependent typecheck must be invalidated.

The formerly selected candidate might remain unchanged throughout. What changes is whether the declaration still has the same grounds for selecting it—or whether a clean build would instead find another outcome, including ambiguity.
Could a candidate become visible even though the edit doesn’t add or modify that candidate?

Conceptually, yes: visibility is a relationship between the candidate and the declaration’s resolution context, not merely an intrinsic property of the candidate. For the negative query to be sound, it must respond to edits that change that relationship as well as edits that add candidates.

The question for the index is therefore not just “which candidate changed?” It is also “which cached searches could have a different visible candidate set after this edit?” The proposal does not specify how the compiler represents or indexes those searches.
Does a trait implementation call for a different sort of negative query than an overload?

The same soundness question applies to both: could a candidate become visible and applicable to a cached declaration’s resolution after an edit? A negative query concerning trait resolution must cover relevant implementations that were absent or inapplicable when the declaration was checked, just as an overload query must cover relevant overloads.

Their concrete visibility and applicability rules may differ in a particular language, so a query cannot assume that one set of rules fits both. The shared requirement is to represent enough of the relevant search that a newly consequential candidate changes the query’s semantic outcome and triggers invalidation.
I worry that indexing only the candidates examined during the old typecheck would miss a newly added implementation.

That worry identifies the central failure mode. An index limited to old candidate identities cannot, by itself, connect a declaration to a candidate that did not yet exist. The negative query has to be associated with the relevant *possibility of a candidate*—the search whose result would change if an applicable implementation appeared.

How broad that association must be depends on the resolution rules and on what the index can safely distinguish. Whatever its form, an edit capable of changing the query’s answer must lead to revalidation. Otherwise the compiler could keep a typecheck that a clean build would resolve differently.
Should the negative query say “no visible candidate” or “no applicable candidate”?

Neither wording is universally sufficient on its own. “No visible candidate” would not describe a successful resolution with one visible candidate and no other applicable alternatives. “No applicable candidate” would be wrong if there is already an applicable selected candidate. A useful negative fact must identify the relevant *alternative or search condition* that the declaration relied on being absent, and preserve the visibility and applicability context needed to reevaluate that fact.

The important test is practical and semantic: if a new overload or trait implementation would alter the clean-build resolution for this declaration, would the recorded query be revalidated and show a changed outcome? The wording of the query is secondary to that coverage.
What if visibility changes but the final applicable set stays the same?

Then the edit may affect the query’s inputs without changing the semantic outcome relevant to the declaration. Revalidation is still important: the compiler should establish that the newly visible candidate is not consequential rather than assume so. If the relevant outcome remains unchanged, the proposal does not call for invalidating the dependent typecheck merely because visibility changed.

That is also why “visibility changed” and “resolution changed” should not be treated as synonyms. Visibility can be an input to resolution; invalidation under this proposal follows a changed semantic outcome of a dependency query.
Could the negative query miss an ambiguity if it checks only whether the old winner is still applicable?

Yes. The old winner can remain applicable while another candidate becomes applicable too. Depending on the language’s resolution rules, a clean build could then report an ambiguity. A query that merely reconfirms the old winner would not test the relevant negative fact: that no alternative changes the resolution outcome.

The query’s semantic comparison must be capable of distinguishing continued unambiguous resolution from an ambiguous result. This is not an extra performance concern; it is necessary to match clean-build diagnostics.
Do we need to record the reason each rejected candidate failed applicability?

The question cannot be settled without specifying the resolution rules and what the query representation can revalidate. Recording a reason might help identify relevant edits, but a stored reason about a known candidate still would not, by itself, account for newly added candidates. Conversely, a query that can soundly recheck the relevant search might not need to store every old rejection reason.

The nonnegotiable part is that the negative fact be tied to enough visibility and applicability context to detect a changed answer. Any representation that misses an edit capable of making a relevant alternative applicable would be insufficient.
So how would you test whether a proposed negative-query representation is expressive enough?

Ask what happens in each direction of change. If a new overload or trait implementation appears, can the index find cached searches to which it could be visible and applicable? If an existing candidate becomes visible, can those searches be found? If a visible candidate becomes applicable, will revalidation recognize the changed outcome? And if a new candidate makes resolution ambiguous, will the dependent declaration be invalidated rather than reused?

Also ask the converse precision question: when an edit cannot change the query’s relevant semantic outcome, can the compiler avoid invalidating the declaration on that basis? Those questions assess the representation against both soundness and reuse, without assuming that a particular query format has already been chosen.
Then the core idea is to make a negative query about a resolution search, not merely a list of unsuccessful candidates?

Yes. The search must be situated in the declaration’s visibility and applicability context, so it can be reconsidered when an edit introduces or changes an overload or trait implementation. Previously rejected candidates may provide useful information, but they are not a substitute for covering candidates that were previously absent.

Revalidation should distinguish a search whose relevant semantic outcome remains unchanged from one whose outcome now affects resolution. The latter invalidates dependent declaration typechecks; the former does not require invalidation on that query alone. The open design question is how to represent and index those negative searches precisely enough to make both distinctions sound.

Here’s a hypothesis for the negative-query problem: scope-qualified candidate-set queries, keyed by overload name or canonical trait goal, will catch newly applicable candidates after index changes. Does that give us the right unit to track?

It is a plausible unit to investigate. The query describes a search space rather than only the candidates that happened to be found before the edit. The overload name or canonical trait goal identifies the kind of resolution being performed, while the scope qualification identifies the context from which candidates can be seen. If an index change can alter the candidate set for that combination, the corresponding query can be revalidated.

The claim remains a hypothesis. It depends on whether those keys and the scope qualification capture every change that could introduce a relevant candidate, and whether revalidation distinguishes a candidate-set change that affects resolution from one that does not.
Why qualify the query by scope instead of keying it only by overload name?

A name alone does not say which candidates are visible to a particular declaration. The same named search could have different answers from different resolution contexts. Scope qualification is intended to connect the query to the context in which the cached declaration was checked, so a new candidate is considered where it could matter without treating every occurrence of that name as the same search.

For the hypothesis to hold, “scope-qualified” has to mean enough to reflect the language’s actual visibility rules. Merely attaching a scope label would not suffice if a visibility-changing edit could alter the search without causing its query to be revisited.
And why use a canonical trait goal as the other key?

The proposed trait key identifies the resolution question in a form that can be matched against index changes. Calling it *canonical* suggests that equivalent presentations of a trait goal should be recognized as the same relevant kind of search, rather than missed because their incidental representations differ.

That does not by itself settle which trait implementations are applicable. The goal key helps locate queries to reconsider; the query must still be interpreted in its scope-qualified context and revalidated when a relevant index change occurs. Whether the chosen canonical form retains everything needed for sound matching is part of what the hypothesis would need to establish.
Is the candidate-set query itself the negative query?

It can serve as the basis for one. A declaration might rely on the absence of any *additional relevant candidate* in the set for its overload name or trait goal. Representing the search as a candidate-set query lets the compiler ask that question again after an index change, including when the candidate did not exist during the earlier typecheck.

The negative fact is not simply an immutable list of rejected candidates. It is a claim about the answer to a search in a particular context. That is the feature the hypothesis offers for detecting a newly applicable overload or trait implementation.
Does a change to the candidate set necessarily mean we have to invalidate the declaration?

No. Under the proposed revalidation approach, a changed index identifies a query that may need another look; it does not establish that the dependent declaration’s resolution has changed. A new candidate could, for example, remain inapplicable to the use in question. Revalidation must determine whether the semantic outcome on which the cached typecheck depends has changed.

The hypothesis is that the scope-qualified, appropriately keyed query will *catch* the possibility of a newly applicable candidate. Catching it for examination is distinct from deciding that the cached declaration must be invalidated.
Then does “candidate-set” mean just a set of visible candidates, or a set of applicable ones?

The hypothesis does not fix that representation. There is a tradeoff in how to state the query: a visible-candidate search still requires checking applicability to the particular use, while a query expressed in terms of applicable candidates must remain sensitive to edits that change applicability even if visibility stays the same.

Whichever interpretation is chosen, it has to cover both ways a new candidate can matter: one may enter the relevant visible search space, or one already in that space may become applicable. The overload-name or canonical-trait-goal key and the scope qualification are proposed ways to locate the relevant search, not a substitute for that semantic check.
What exactly does “after index changes” contribute to the hypothesis?

It places the proposed detection point at changes to the indexed candidate information. An edit that can change the indexed answer for a scope-qualified overload-name or canonical-trait-goal query should cause that query to be reconsidered. This is how a newly introduced candidate could be noticed even though the earlier cached typecheck had no dependency on that candidate’s identity.

The phrase does not specify the index’s data structure or prove that every relevant edit changes the index in a detectable way. Coverage of such changes is one of the conditions the hypothesis would have to satisfy.
Suppose an overload is added under the same name, but it isn’t visible from the declaration’s scope. What should this hypothesis predict?

The scope qualification should make that distinction relevant. The addition might be associated with the name in some broader index, but revalidating the declaration’s scope-qualified query should find no change to the candidate set that matters from that context. On this resolution dependency, it would not justify invalidating the cached typecheck.

That is a desired precision property of the proposed keying, not an established property of an unspecified index. The design would have to ensure that its notion of scope corresponds to the visibility rules used by a clean build.
Now suppose the candidate is visible but not applicable. Can a candidate-set query still be useful?

Yes, provided the subsequent semantic comparison accounts for applicability. The query could be flagged and revalidated because the visible search space changed, while the declaration’s resolution outcome remains the same because the new candidate does not apply. In that case the query has helped establish that invalidation is unnecessary on this ground.

If the representation instead calls the candidate-set outcome unchanged without ever checking whether a candidate has become applicable, it would fail the purpose of the hypothesis. Visibility is a way to locate the search; applicability is part of deciding whether its answer matters to the cached result.
Could an existing trait implementation become applicable without the index gaining a new implementation?

That is an important question for the hypothesis. If an edit can change whether an existing implementation applies to a canonical trait goal, the relevant query still has to be revisited. Keying only on the addition or removal of implementation identities would not cover that situation.

So “after index changes” has to be understood broadly enough to include detectable changes to indexed information that can affect the query’s answer. If the proposed index cannot expose an applicability change, the keying scheme alone would not establish that newly applicable candidates are caught.
Does canonicalizing the trait goal risk treating two resolution contexts as identical?

It could if the canonical key erased information that affects which implementations participate or apply. Scope qualification is meant to preserve contextual distinctions, but the combination must still be checked against the actual resolution semantics. Two queries should be combined for indexing only insofar as doing so will not cause a relevant change for either to be missed.

Conversely, treating semantically equivalent searches as unrelated could increase revalidation work. The hypothesis leaves the precise equivalence relation open; it identifies the proposed key, not a demonstrated canonicalization rule.
Where would a new ambiguity show up?

The index change should lead to revalidation of the affected scope-qualified query. If a new candidate is now applicable and the resulting resolution is ambiguous, that is a changed semantic outcome for the dependent declaration. Its cached typecheck would need to be invalidated so the incremental build can produce the clean-build diagnostic.

Simply noticing that the old selected candidate remains in the set would not be enough. The candidate-set query is useful only if revalidation considers the consequences of additional candidates, including ambiguity.
Would it be fair to say this hypothesis solves the problem of candidates that weren’t present in the old cache?

It is fair to say that it is *aimed at* that problem. A query keyed to a search can be found after a new candidate appears, whereas a dependency solely on old candidate identities cannot name that candidate in advance. The proposed scope, overload-name, and canonical-trait-goal information could give the index a route from a change to the searches it may affect.

It is not yet fair to claim that route is complete. The hypothesis would need to cover visibility changes, applicability changes, and any relevant distinction lost in the keys, as well as additions of candidate identities.
What should we examine to decide whether the hypothesis really catches newly applicable candidates?

For each kind of edit that could change overload or trait resolution, ask whether it changes indexed information associated with every affected scope-qualified name or canonical goal. Then ask whether revalidating that query recognizes when the candidate becomes applicable and when that changes the declaration’s semantic resolution outcome. A missed route from edit to query is a soundness failure; a route that revalidates extra queries may instead be a precision or cost concern.

The hypothesis would be supported only if those checks cover candidates newly introduced into the search and existing candidates newly made relevant, including cases that produce ambiguity. That is a way to assess it, not a claim that the assessment has already been done.
How does this relate to the reuse target without assuming we’ve achieved it?

Scope qualification and query revalidation are intended to avoid discarding a declaration merely because an index changed somewhere under the same name or trait. They offer a way to keep a cached typecheck when its relevant resolution-query outcome remains semantically unchanged, while still finding a newly applicable candidate where one matters.

Whether that precision is sufficient to reuse at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged remains an open question. The hypothesis identifies a possible dependency key and detection mechanism; it does not supply a reuse measurement or a proof of clean-build equivalence.
So the claim I’m proposing is about which searches to revisit, not that every matching index update changes the answer?

Right. The proposed claim is that scope-qualified candidate-set queries keyed by overload name or canonical trait goal will bring the right searches back for revalidation after index changes, including searches that can gain a newly applicable overload or trait implementation. Matching an update to a query means “check this”; it does not mean “invalidate its declaration.” Invalidation follows if the revalidated semantic outcome changes.

The remaining question is whether that proposed mapping is complete and precise under the compiler’s visibility and applicability rules. Until then, it should remain a hypothesis rather than a guaranteed solution.

I want to turn the negative-query question into a plan: index scoped name queries and unification-compatible trait-goal queries, including queries whose candidate sets are empty. After visibility or implementation edits, recheck the affected resolutions. Can we unpack what that commits us to?

The plan commits to recording searches, not just references to candidates found during an earlier typecheck. A scoped name query describes a name search from a particular resolution context. A unification-compatible trait-goal query describes a search for implementations that could match a trait goal. Including empty sets matters because an empty search still conveys a fact the typecheck may rely on; a later edit could make its answer nonempty.

The second part is an action after edits: visibility or implementation changes prompt rechecking of resolutions that the indexed queries identify as potentially affected. The plan does not, by itself, establish that every relevant resolution will be found or that rechecking will be cheap. Those are obligations for the proposed indexing and recheck mechanism.
Why explicitly include empty sets? Isn’t there nothing to index in that case?

There may be no candidate identity to index, but there is still a query to index. If a declaration’s resolution depended on a scoped name search finding nothing, or on a trait-goal search having no unification-compatible implementation, that absence can cease to hold after an edit. Omitting empty results would make the searches most vulnerable to newly appearing candidates difficult to revisit.

So the index entry is for the search and its context, even when its current candidate set is empty. The plan does not require pretending that an absent candidate has an identity.
What is the significance of “scoped” in a scoped name query?

It anchors the name search to the context from which resolution took place. A name occurring in two different contexts need not have the same visible candidates. A visibility edit might affect one search but not the other, so indexing just the name could be too blunt—or, if it overlooks a contextual change, unsound.

The exact representation of that context is not settled by the word “scoped.” The requirement for the plan is that it be sufficient to find the resolutions whose relevant visibility may have changed.
For traits, why say “unification-compatible trait-goal queries” rather than just index the trait name?

A trait name alone may describe a broader search than the goal a declaration actually tries to resolve. The plan uses unification compatibility to identify implementations that could matter to that goal. That gives the index a way to associate an implementation edit with potentially affected goal queries without relying solely on the identities of implementations already found.

Compatibility here is a filter for deciding what needs consideration, not a promise that every compatible implementation ultimately applies or changes the resolution. Rechecking is still needed to determine the edited program’s actual resolution outcome.
Could the index exclude an implementation because it wasn’t applicable during the old typecheck?

It must not use old inapplicability as a reason to overlook an edit that could make the implementation relevant. The plan’s unification-compatible trait-goal queries are meant to identify searches to revisit when implementation information changes, including cases where an old resolution depended on a negative result.

At the same time, “unification-compatible” is not a complete definition of applicability. The plan would need to ensure that whatever it indexes and rechecks covers changes capable of altering the resolution. An index that captures only previously selected implementations would not satisfy that purpose.
Is indexing an empty trait-goal set useful even if an implementation edit later adds something that doesn’t actually apply?

Yes. The empty query can provide a route from the edit to a resolution worth checking. Rechecking may then establish that the new or changed implementation does not alter the relevant outcome. Being flagged as potentially affected is different from being proved changed.

The aim is to avoid missing a consequential addition without requiring every potentially related implementation edit to invalidate the cached declaration. That distinction is especially important when trying to preserve typechecking results whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged.
What exactly happens after a visibility edit under this plan?

The index is used to identify scoped name queries whose resolution might now differ, and the affected resolutions are rechecked against the edited program. A visibility edit matters because it can change which overloads a declaration can see even when the declaration’s source and the overloads themselves are unchanged.

The plan does not specify the internal form of a visibility edit or a particular index data structure. Its soundness depends on finding every resolution whose relevant visible search space could have changed, including searches that previously returned an empty set.
And after an implementation edit?

The corresponding task is to identify trait-goal queries for which the implementation edit could affect resolution, using the planned unification-compatible indexing, and recheck those resolutions. A changed implementation might affect a goal even if that implementation was not the previous resolution result.

As with visibility edits, finding a query for rechecking does not mean the declaration’s semantic outcome necessarily changes. The recheck establishes whether it does.
Does the wording limit us to edits that add candidates?

No. The plan names visibility or implementation edits, not only additions. Such edits can change which candidates are considered or how resolution proceeds. Including empty sets makes additions particularly clear, but the instruction to recheck affected resolutions applies whenever those edits could change their outcomes.

The plan does not enumerate every possible edit in a compiler. It identifies these edit categories because they can affect the name and trait-goal searches being indexed.
What if a candidate is already visible and an implementation edit changes whether it works for a goal?

That is a case the trait-goal side needs to handle. The index should lead the edit to queries whose goals could be affected, and rechecking the resolution must determine whether applicability or the final outcome changed. Merely comparing a before-and-after list of implementation identities would not answer that question.

The plan says to index unification-compatible trait-goal queries and recheck resolutions after implementation edits; it does not say that a candidate-set identity comparison replaces resolution.
Is the index recording a final resolution, a set of candidates, or the query that produced them?

The plan specifically calls for indexing *queries*: scoped name queries and unification-compatible trait-goal queries. Their results, including empty candidate sets, matter because they explain what the cached typecheck depended on. The final resolution is what needs reconsideration after an edit may affect one of those queries.

That distinction prevents a common gap: a final resolution alone says little about a candidate that was absent before the edit. A query can be revisited when that candidate appears, provided the edit-to-query indexing is sound.
Do we recheck every resolution that has the same name as an edited overload?

The plan calls for *scoped* name queries, so matching by name alone is not the full criterion. A recheck is needed where a visibility edit could affect the resolution from that query’s scope. The index may conservatively identify extra queries, but treating every use of a name as changed would lose the distinction the scope qualification is meant to preserve.

Conversely, scope qualification must not be so narrow that a newly visible overload fails to reach a declaration whose resolution it could affect. The plan sets that coverage requirement without specifying an index layout.
When we say “recheck resolutions,” are we merely checking whether the new candidate set is identical?

No. Candidate-set changes are a reason to examine a resolution, but identical candidate identities are not automatically proof of an identical outcome, particularly after an implementation edit. The recheck has to determine the resolution outcome under the edited program using the applicable rules. That includes recognizing if an added or newly applicable candidate produces ambiguity.

For reuse, the relevant distinction is whether the semantic resolution dependency remains unchanged, not whether the index’s stored list looks the same. The plan has not fixed how that semantic comparison is represented.
Could a resolution be rechecked and its cached declaration typecheck still be kept?

Yes. Rechecking means an edit might matter; it is not itself a finding that the typecheck is stale. If the rechecked resolution has the same relevant semantic outcome, the edit supplies no reason on that resolution dependency alone to discard the cached result. If it changes, the dependent result has to be reconsidered to preserve clean-build diagnostics and executable behavior.

That is the intended separation between precise detection and precise invalidation. The plan supplies a way to locate resolutions for examination, including ones with previously empty searches; it does not equate every recheck with invalidation.
Suppose an empty scoped name query becomes nonempty after a visibility edit. Is invalidation automatic?

The change means the resolution needs to be rechecked; it does not by itself settle the final outcome. Whether the newly visible candidate applies and whether it changes selection or creates ambiguity depends on the resolution rules. If the semantic outcome changes, the dependent declaration typecheck cannot be reused unchanged. If it does not, a nonempty search alone need not force invalidation on that dependency.

This is why the plan includes both indexing empty queries and rechecking resolutions. Indexing catches the possibility of change; rechecking determines its consequence.
What about an empty trait-goal query that gains a unification-compatible implementation?

It follows the same pattern. Because the empty goal query was indexed, the implementation edit can cause the affected resolution to be revisited. Unification compatibility marks it as potentially relevant, not necessarily as a successful or uniquely selected implementation. The recheck determines what the edited goal resolves to, including whether there is a new ambiguity.

Without an entry for the empty query, there would be no previously found implementation to serve as a dependency, which is exactly the gap this part of the plan addresses.
How do we know whether the proposed index has sufficient coverage?

A useful way to examine the plan is to ask, for each visibility edit that could change a declaration’s name resolution, whether its scoped name query is located for rechecking. Ask the analogous question for each implementation edit that could change a trait goal: does its unification-compatible goal query get located, including when the prior set was empty? Then verify that rechecking can recognize changed outcomes rather than merely changed candidate identities.

Those are checks the plan calls for; they are not results already established. Missing an affected query would put clean-build equivalence at risk, while rechecking too many unaffected queries would raise a precision concern.
Is the choice of unification compatibility meant to prove an implementation applies?

No. It is a way to describe which trait-goal queries an implementation edit might affect. Final applicability and resolution still require a recheck in the declaration’s relevant context. Conflating compatibility with a final successful resolution could cause the compiler to invalidate needlessly or to report the wrong outcome.

The soundness obligation is that compatibility-based indexing not miss an edit capable of changing a goal’s resolution. The precision obligation is to avoid broad rechecking where the index can safely distinguish unrelated goals.
Does this plan already establish that we can reach at least 95% reuse?

No. It specifies which queries to index—including empty ones—and when to recheck potentially affected resolutions. Those choices are intended to help preserve typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged, while catching newly relevant overloads and implementations.

Whether the compiler actually reuses at least 95% of typechecking results for that class of declarations remains to be shown. The plan also needs to meet the independent correctness requirement: across edits, diagnostics and executable behavior must match a clean build.
Can you state the distinction between the two kinds of queries one more time without assuming a particular language?

A *scoped name query* asks about candidates for a name from a particular visibility context; it provides a way to revisit overload resolution when visibility changes. A *unification-compatible trait-goal query* asks about implementations that could be relevant to a particular goal; it provides a way to revisit trait resolution when implementation information changes. In either case the query is indexed even if its current candidate set is empty.

Those descriptions identify potentially affected searches. They do not define a language’s visibility rules, prove trait applicability, or choose the final resolution. That is why the plan pairs the index with rechecking after the specified edits.
So the plan’s immediate purpose is to avoid making old candidate identities the only way an edit reaches a cached declaration?

Yes. Indexing scoped name and unification-compatible trait-goal *queries*, including empty sets, gives an edit a potential route to a cached declaration’s resolution even when the relevant overload or implementation was absent before. Rechecking after visibility or implementation edits then determines whether that possibility actually changes the resolution. Whether those routes are complete and precise enough remains an open property of the proposed design.

Let’s run ResolutionFlip-1000 with overload and blanket-impl edits. I want to compare the cached build’s diagnostics and executable behavior against clean builds, and measure reuse for unchanged declarations. What does that activity actually test?

It tests two things separately. The clean-build comparisons test whether caching remains sound when overload or trait resolution can change after an edit. The reuse measurement tests whether declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged retain their typechecking results rather than being rechecked unnecessarily.

The activity is an evaluation, not a result. Running ResolutionFlip-1000 could reveal either a correctness mismatch or excessive invalidation; the node does not say what it will find.

They exercise the two kinds of resolution the design needs to handle. An overload edit can affect which named candidates participate in a declaration’s resolution. The comparison with a clean build asks whether the incremental path notices the consequential changes. The reuse measurement asks whether it avoids discarding results when the relevant dependencies do not change semantically.

For an edited program, compare the diagnostics produced by the cached incremental path with those produced by a clean build of that same edited program. The requirement is to match clean-build diagnostics, not just to detect that some resolution was affected.

That includes the possibility that an edit makes an additional candidate applicable and a clean build reports ambiguity. Retaining an earlier successful resolution in that situation would be a mismatch even if the cached declaration’s own source had not changed.

Matching diagnostics alone would not establish that a reused typechecking result leads to the same executable behavior as a clean build. The activity therefore checks both observable sides named in the goal. It does not assume that one comparison is a substitute for the other.
If an edit creates an ambiguity, there might not be an executable. How should I read the behavior comparison in that case?

The diagnostic comparison still applies: the cached path must reflect the ambiguity that a clean build reports. The executable-behavior comparison applies where the edited program yields an executable whose behavior can be compared. The absence of an executable in an ambiguous case does not excuse a diagnostic mismatch, and a matching ambiguity diagnostic does not eliminate the need to compare behavior in cases that do produce executables.

The edits give it something to be tested against. If a newly applicable overload or implementation changes a clean-build resolution, the indexed query approach is meant to lead the incremental path to reconsider the affected declaration. The clean-build comparison can expose a failure to do so.

Conversely, if the resolution dependencies of a declaration remain semantically unchanged, the reuse measurement can show whether indexing and rechecking preserve its cached typechecking result. The activity evaluates those expectations; it does not establish in advance that the queries catch every change.
Could the cached build match the clean build yet still do badly on this evaluation?

Yes. Rechecking every declaration could protect against stale cached results, but it would not demonstrate the desired reuse. That is why the activity measures unchanged-declaration reuse as well as comparing diagnostics and behavior.

The stated target is to reuse at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. Correct outputs by themselves do not show that the target is met.
Could high reuse coexist with a failed clean-build comparison?

Yes. Keeping a stale result could increase the reuse count while hiding a newly applicable candidate or an ambiguity. That would fail the soundness requirement regardless of the reuse percentage. The measurements need to remain separate so an impressive cache-hit figure does not mask a difference in diagnostics or executable behavior.
When measuring unchanged-declaration reuse, is an unchanged source declaration automatically in the denominator?

Not automatically. A declaration’s text can stay unchanged while an overload or implementation edit changes its resolution dependencies. The stated reuse target concerns declarations whose resolution dependencies remain *semantically unchanged*. The activity’s unchanged-declaration measurement needs to be interpreted with that condition in mind; source text alone does not establish it.

Otherwise a case that legitimately needs rechecking after a cross-module resolution change could be counted as a reuse failure, or a stale result could be credited as successful reuse.
Suppose an edit affects an indexed query, but rechecking yields the same semantic resolution outcome. What should the activity tell us?

For that resolution dependency, the edit presented a possibility of change that did not materialize. The declaration is relevant to the precision side of the evaluation if its resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged: can the incremental compiler reuse its typechecking result rather than invalidate it solely because the query needed rechecking?

The clean-build comparisons still apply. An unchanged query outcome is useful evidence for reuse, but it does not replace checking that cached diagnostics and executable behavior match the clean build.
What would an overload edit reveal if a query recorded only the previously selected candidate?

If the edit made another candidate applicable, a dependency solely on the old selection might not cause the cached declaration to be revisited. A clean build could then reach a different resolution or report an ambiguity while the cached path retains its prior result. Comparing diagnostics and executable behavior is intended to expose that kind of mismatch.

Whether ResolutionFlip-1000 actually exposes one is a question for the run; it is not an outcome we can assert beforehand.
What is distinctive about exercising blanket-impl edits in the same evaluation?

They give the evaluation a way to probe trait-goal resolution rather than relying only on named overload searches. An implementation edit may alter which candidate is relevant to a goal even when the dependent declaration is untouched. The same correctness question follows: does the cached path agree with a clean build after the edit?

The activity does not state what any particular blanket-impl edit does to a resolution. Its role is to include that kind of change in the evaluation.
Do we need to call every recheck an invalidation when interpreting the reuse figure?

No. Rechecking a potentially affected resolution and discarding a declaration’s cached typechecking result are different actions. The proposed approach uses rechecking to determine whether a semantic outcome changed; if it did not, the dependent result may remain reusable on that ground.

For the reuse measurement, the question is whether the typechecking result was actually reused for a declaration in the target class. Counting every query recheck as a lost declaration typecheck would blur that distinction.
How should I state a pass condition without reporting results that we don’t have yet?

State what will be compared and measured. Across the ResolutionFlip-1000 overload and blanket-impl edits, compare cached diagnostics and executable behavior with clean builds, and measure reuse of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. The goal is clean-build agreement, including newly applicable candidates and ambiguities, alongside at least 95% reuse in that target class.

That specifies the criteria for interpreting the run without claiming that either criterion has been met.
If we see a discrepancy, can we already say which part of the query design caused it?

No. A discrepancy would show that the cached path did not match the clean build for that edit, but the comparison alone would not establish its cause. Similarly, a reuse shortfall would establish that the measured target was not met, not by itself which indexing or invalidation choice was responsible.

ResolutionFlip-1000 is the activity for evaluating the approach. Diagnosing a particular outcome would require evidence from the run, which we do not have here.
So the evaluation has to notice both needless rechecking and missed resolution changes?

Yes. Comparing cached diagnostics and behavior against clean builds addresses missed changes that affect correctness. Measuring unchanged-declaration reuse addresses unnecessary loss of cached typechecking results. The overload and blanket-impl edits put both concerns in the setting where candidates can become newly relevant across edits.

Keeping those observations distinct will let the activity test soundness and reuse without treating either one as proof of the other.

No inherent tension. Rechecking whether a resolution query changed is distinct from discarding a declaration’s cached typechecking result. A query may be revisited after an edit yet yield the same relevant semantic outcome, allowing the dependent typechecking result to be reused on that ground.

I’m ready to adopt scoped positive and negative candidate-set dependencies for cached declaration typechecks. The decision is supported by ResolutionFlip-1000 parity and 97.2% unchanged-dependency reuse. How should we state what we’re adopting?

State the decision as adopting **scoped positive and negative candidate-set dependencies**. A cached declaration typecheck depends both on relevant candidates that resolution found and on relevant candidate-set facts about what was absent or did not affect the result, interpreted from the declaration’s scope. That lets an edit be checked against the resolution search rather than only against the identity of a previously selected candidate.

The stated support is ResolutionFlip-1000 parity with clean builds and 97.2% reuse for declarations whose resolution dependencies remained semantically unchanged. That supports the choice without turning the decision into a claim that every possible edit has been tested.

A positive dependency captures a fact about candidates resolution did find or use. A negative dependency captures a relevant absence or non-applicability that also helps justify the result. If the compiler records only the positive side, a new overload or trait implementation could matter even though the previously selected candidate stays the same.

Adopting both means the dependency model accounts for changes to the candidate set, including changes that challenge an earlier absence claim. It does not mean every candidate-set change necessarily changes the declaration’s final resolution.

It ties a candidate-set dependency to the resolution context of the declaration. Visibility can differ between contexts, so a name or goal alone does not necessarily identify the candidate set relevant to a particular typecheck. Scope is part of stating which search the cached result relied on.

The decision names that property of the dependencies; it does not, by itself, specify a particular representation of scope or an index data structure.
Should I describe this as adopting the previously discussed query index wholesale?

The narrower, faithful statement is that you’re adopting scoped positive and negative **candidate-set dependencies**. Queries and indexing explain how such dependencies might be recorded and revisited, but this decision does not spell out every detail of an index or commit to a particular query representation.

It is useful to preserve that distinction: the decision identifies what cached typechecks must depend on, while implementation details remain details unless they are stated as part of the decision.
Does the decision imply that an edit to any candidate in the scope invalidates a declaration?

No. A dependency gives the compiler a reason to examine whether an edit changes a relevant semantic outcome. It need not treat every potentially relevant edit as a changed resolution. The positive and negative candidate-set facts are meant to distinguish a genuinely changed dependency from one that remains semantically unchanged.

That distinction matters to the reported reuse figure: 97.2% refers to unchanged-dependency reuse, not to invalidating every declaration connected to an edited scope.

If a reader needs clarification, the parity concerns the cached path matching clean builds on diagnostics and executable behavior in that evaluation. You do not need to restate a full account of the evaluation to express the decision.

Keep the wording tied to the evaluation rather than promoting its observed parity into an unrestricted guarantee about all edits.
Is 97.2% a reuse rate over all declaration typechecks?

No. The decision calls it **unchanged-dependency reuse**. Its meaning is reuse of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remained semantically unchanged. Rephrasing it as a percentage of all declarations would change the claim.
Does choosing this dependency model mean the compiler may reuse a result whenever its old selected candidate still exists?

No. The negative candidate-set dependencies are there precisely because the continued existence of an old selected candidate does not settle whether resolution is still the same. Another candidate could become relevant, potentially changing the outcome or creating an ambiguity.

Should we say the decision proves clean-build equivalence?

What if someone reads “negative dependency” as meaning we’re caching an error?

Yes. That contrast captures a central part of the decision. An individual-candidate dependency can describe something already known, but a scoped candidate-set dependency can describe the relevant search even when a consequential candidate was not previously present.

The decision includes both positive and negative facts about that search. It does not require claiming that the candidate set alone, without the rest of typechecking’s requirements, is sufficient to reuse an entire result.
Are overload resolution and trait resolution both covered by this decision?

The decision is framed for the resolution problem that includes overload and trait candidates. Scoped candidate-set dependencies are intended to make cached declaration typechecks responsive to relevant changes in either kind of search, including a newly relevant alternative.

Precision in reuse comes from distinguishing unchanged semantic dependencies from changed ones, not from dropping an absence fact simply because there is no candidate identity to record.

Keeping them separate prevents an observed evaluation result from being mistaken for the definition of the dependency model, or the decision from being mistaken for an additional measurement.
