“Adopt scoped positive and negative candidate-set dependencies for cached declaration typechecks, supported by ResolutionFlip-1000 clean-build parity and 97.2% unchanged-dependency reuse.”

For implementation, I want to use the chosen candidate-set dependencies with signature and visibility fingerprints, then perform selective rechecks. The acceptance requirements are clean-build diagnostic and execution parity and at least 95% reuse. How should I frame that plan?

Frame it as a plan to implement the chosen candidate-set dependencies, use signature and visibility fingerprints to identify changes that may matter to them, and selectively recheck affected resolutions before deciding whether cached declaration typechecks can be reused. The fingerprints are a way to notice possible changes; a recheck determines whether the relevant semantic outcome actually changed.

Keep the acceptance conditions explicit and separate: the incremental compiler must match a clean build’s diagnostics and executable behavior across edits, and it must reuse at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. The plan has not yet established that the implementation satisfies either condition.
What role does a signature fingerprint play in that description?

It is intended to help identify edits to signature information that could affect a candidate-set dependency. If such information changes in a way relevant to an overload or trait resolution, a cached conclusion should not be retained merely because its declaration’s source is untouched.

The word “fingerprint” does not itself guarantee soundness. The implementation has to ensure that differences capable of changing resolution are detected and lead to appropriate rechecks. The plan does not specify a fingerprint format or claim that every signature change necessarily changes a resolution.
And a visibility fingerprint is for changes to which candidates a declaration can see?

That is the intended distinction. Visibility can change the candidates participating in a declaration’s resolution even if their signatures do not change. A visibility fingerprint is meant to help flag candidate-set dependencies that may need rechecking when that context changes.

The two fingerprint categories should not be mistaken for two independent proofs of reuse. A cached typecheck is safe only if the resolution dependencies it relies on remain semantically valid; fingerprints help route potentially relevant edits to that determination.
Does selective rechecking mean we invalidate every declaration whose fingerprint changes?

No. Selective rechecking means using change information to decide which resolutions need another look, rather than immediately discarding every potentially affected declaration typecheck. A changed fingerprint may indicate that a dependency *could* have changed. The recheck asks whether its relevant semantic outcome did change.

If it did, the dependent cached typecheck must be reconsidered. If it did not, that particular resolution dependency does not require invalidation. Other dependencies still have to be respected; an unchanged resolution answer alone is not a blanket permission to reuse an entire typecheck.
Could we skip the recheck when a signature fingerprint is unchanged?

Only if the fingerprint scheme and the other required dependency checks establish that no relevant change was missed. An unchanged signature fingerprint alone says nothing about a visibility change, and it must not be treated as proof about information it does not cover.

The implementation obligation is to make the combination of dependency tracking, fingerprints, and selective rechecks sound. If a relevant edit can leave the checked fingerprints unchanged, the compiler needs another way to recognize it or it risks reusing a stale result.
I want the implementation to stay selective without losing a newly applicable overload or trait implementation. Where is that tension handled?

It is handled at both stages. The fingerprints and dependency matching must cause a relevant candidate-set query to be reconsidered when an edit could make a candidate newly applicable, including a candidate absent from the earlier result. Then the recheck must distinguish an actual change in resolution from a potential change that proves irrelevant.

Making the first stage too narrow threatens clean-build parity; making it too broad, or invalidating on potential impact alone, threatens the reuse requirement. The plan calls for selectivity while requiring correctness, not for optimizing either measure at the expense of the other.
How do negative candidate-set dependencies fit alongside the fingerprints?

They specify relevant facts of absence or non-applicability on which a cached declaration typecheck depends. A fingerprint can help signal an edit that might make one of those facts false. Rechecking the associated resolution then determines whether a newly visible or applicable candidate changes the semantic outcome.

Without the negative dependency, a change that introduces an alternative might have no route to a cached typecheck if the cache remembers only the old selected candidate. Without adequate change detection, merely recording the negative dependency would not ensure it gets reconsidered. The plan needs both pieces to work together.
Do positive candidate-set dependencies need the same treatment?

Yes. Information about candidates already participating in resolution can change, and the affected resolution may need rechecking. The distinction is that negative dependencies also cover relevant alternatives that were absent or did not apply before the edit. Both belong to the chosen candidate-set dependency model.

Signature and visibility fingerprints are proposed aids for finding potentially changed dependencies. Neither the positive nor the negative side should be treated as permanently valid just because the cached declaration itself has not been edited.
What does “clean-build diagnostic parity” demand if a recheck discovers ambiguity?

The incremental path must produce the diagnostics a clean build would produce for the edited program. It cannot retain a prior successful resolution and omit an ambiguity diagnostic simply because the earlier typecheck was cached. Rechecking must feed the changed resolution into whatever reconsideration is necessary to obtain the clean-build diagnostic outcome.

This is a requirement on the implementation, not an assertion that the planned fingerprints and rechecks have already met it.
Why name execution parity separately from diagnostics?

Because matching what the compiler reports does not by itself establish that an executable built incrementally behaves as a clean-built executable would. A stale resolution could affect executable behavior without being exposed by the diagnostic comparison. The plan therefore requires both kinds of parity where executable behavior can be compared.

In a case where the edited program does not yield an executable, the diagnostic requirement still applies. The two conditions address different observable consequences of reuse.
Does the ≥95% requirement mean that 95% of all declarations must be reused after every edit?

No. The stated reuse requirement is **at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged**. It is not a per-edit guarantee about all declarations, nor does unchanged source text alone define eligibility.

The plan should measure reuse in that specified population. Declarations whose resolution dependencies do change may need rechecking for correctness; reusing them simply to raise the percentage would not satisfy the plan.
If an edit changes a visibility fingerprint but the rechecked candidate-set outcome stays the same, should that count against reuse?

The fingerprint change alone should not force loss of the cached declaration typecheck. If the relevant resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged, selective rechecking is meant to preserve reuse on that ground. Whether the entire result can be reused still depends on its other applicable dependencies.

For the ≥95% measure, the meaningful question is whether the eligible typechecking result was reused, not whether a fingerprint was inspected or a resolution query was rechecked along the way.
Could we treat equal fingerprints as equivalent to matching clean-build outputs?

No. Fingerprints are part of the proposed implementation mechanism, while clean-build diagnostic and execution parity are observable acceptance requirements. Equal fingerprints are useful only to the extent that they soundly establish that relevant information has not changed. They do not replace checking the incremental result against the clean-build behavior required by the plan.

The same distinction applies when fingerprints differ: a difference may call for rechecking, but it does not automatically imply a different diagnostic or executable outcome.
How specific should we be about what the signature and visibility fingerprints contain?

The plan commits to using signature and visibility fingerprints, but it does not define their contents or encoding. We can state the responsibility each has: changes relevant to resolution must not be hidden from selective rechecking. We should not present a particular fingerprint layout or equality rule as already chosen.

A useful way to keep the plan precise without inventing those details is to phrase the invariant: any edit capable of changing a cached candidate-set dependency must either be detected through the fingerprint-based mechanism or otherwise cause its resolution to be reconsidered.
Is rechecking a resolution the same thing as re-typechecking its whole declaration?

Not necessarily. The plan distinguishes selective resolution rechecks from reuse of declaration typechecking results. A potentially affected resolution can be examined to see whether its semantic outcome changed. If it remains unchanged and the other grounds for reuse hold, retaining the cached declaration typecheck is consistent with the plan. If it changes, the cached result cannot simply be retained unchanged.

The plan does not mandate a particular internal granularity for rechecking or specify how much work a changed resolution requires. Its requirements are sound results and the stated reuse level.
What would count as a failure of selectivity even if diagnostics and executable behavior matched?

If the implementation discards too many typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged, it can fail the **at-least-95% reuse** condition while still matching clean builds. For example, treating every potentially affected fingerprint as a reason for unconditional declaration invalidation could lose reusable results.

Parity and reuse are independent acceptance conditions. Passing the correctness comparison does not waive the reuse threshold, just as reaching the threshold does not excuse a diagnostic or behavioral mismatch.
Can the plan be described as complete now that we have a dependency model and fingerprints?

It can be described as a concrete implementation plan, not as a completed implementation or a demonstrated outcome. The chosen candidate-set dependencies identify what must be tracked; signature and visibility fingerprints are intended to help identify relevant edits; selective rechecks determine whether affected resolutions actually changed. The stated diagnostic, execution, and reuse requirements still have to be met by the implementation.

That wording preserves the distinction between the mechanism being planned and the conditions under which it would be acceptable.
Give me a compact implementation directive that retains the acceptance conditions.

Implement the chosen scoped positive and negative candidate-set dependencies using signature and visibility fingerprints to drive selective resolution rechecks. Require parity with clean builds for diagnostics and executable behavior across edits, including newly applicable candidates and ambiguities, and reuse at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged.

For TypeCache v2, implement reverse-indexed scoped candidate queries, keep records even when a query returns an empty set, and perform selective rechecks after signature, visibility, or impl edits. Can we spell out what this implementation activity entails?

It has three connected parts. TypeCache v2 needs to retain scoped candidate queries associated with cached typechecking results. It needs a reverse index so an edit can lead back to queries it may affect. And it needs to recheck the relevant resolutions selectively after signature, visibility, or implementation edits.

An empty result still needs a record: a later edit might change that search from empty to nonempty. The activity specifies those capabilities, but does not yet report that they have been implemented or tested.
What does “reverse-indexed” mean in this setting?

It describes the direction of lookup after an edit. Instead of starting with a cached declaration and asking what it depended on, the compiler needs to start with changed information and find the scoped candidate queries that might depend on it. Those queries identify resolutions worth rechecking.

The term does not prescribe a particular data structure. What matters is that the reverse lookup reaches a query when the edit could change its answer, including when the answer was previously empty.
Why index the query rather than just the candidate it returned?

A returned candidate can be tracked by identity, but that does not describe the whole search. A new candidate cannot already appear in a cached list of returned candidates. Indexing the scoped query gives an edit a route to the search itself, so the resolution can be reconsidered when its candidate set might change.

That distinction is especially important for an empty result: there is no returned candidate to index, yet the absence may have been relevant to a cached typecheck.
Does a scoped candidate query have to return at least one candidate to become a dependency?

No. TypeCache v2 is to retain **empty-set records** as well. A query that found no candidates can still express a relevant resolution fact. If the compiler dropped that record, a later signature, visibility, or impl edit might make the search consequential without any old candidate identity connecting the edit to the cached result.
When an edit arrives, does finding a query through the reverse index mean its declaration must immediately be invalidated?

No. Finding the query means the edit may have affected its resolution. The selective recheck determines whether the relevant semantic outcome changed. Treating every reverse-index match as an automatic declaration invalidation would remove the distinction between possible impact and actual change.

The implementation activity calls for selective rechecks, not unconditional invalidation on every index hit.
How do signature edits enter that flow?

A signature edit is one of the edit categories that should prompt lookup of potentially affected scoped candidate queries. A change in signature information can affect whether a candidate matters to a resolution, so TypeCache v2 must not rely only on whether the declaration being typechecked changed.

The reverse lookup identifies queries to consider; rechecking determines the resolution under the edited information. The activity does not specify a particular signature representation or say that every signature edit changes an outcome.
What is different about a visibility edit?

A visibility edit can change which candidates participate in a search from a particular scope. That makes the scope on the cached query important: the same candidate-related change need not affect every declaration’s search in the same way.

TypeCache v2 needs to find scoped queries whose visibility context could have changed and recheck their resolutions. A query whose answer remains semantically unchanged need not be treated as changed just because a visibility edit triggered its recheck.
And “impl edits” refers to the implementation side of trait resolution?

Yes. An impl edit can change what is relevant to a trait-resolution query. The reverse index is meant to find potentially affected scoped candidate queries, including searches that previously had empty results, so their resolutions can be rechecked.

The activity does not say that every impl edit creates an applicable candidate. It says to perform selective rechecks after edits of that kind where they may affect cached resolution.
Could a single edit lead to more than one cached query?

Conceptually, yes. Reverse indexing is useful precisely because an edit may be relevant to multiple cached searches, while other searches remain unrelated. Each potentially affected resolution needs the appropriate recheck; the edit itself is not a reason to discard all cached typechecks.

The activity does not prescribe how queries are grouped or how many an edit should reach. Its requirement is that relevant ones not be missed and that rechecking remain selective.
If a query was empty before and is nonempty after an edit, can we stop at that comparison?

That change makes the old absence fact worth reconsidering, but a nonempty candidate set alone does not settle the final resolution. The new candidate might or might not affect applicability or the outcome. TypeCache v2’s selective recheck has to determine what the edited resolution means for the cached typecheck.

Keeping the empty-set record is what makes the transition discoverable. Rechecking is what determines its consequence.
What if the query returns the same candidate identities after an impl edit?

The identity list alone may not answer whether the resolution’s semantic outcome remains the same. An impl edit is specifically a reason to consider whether the implementation information relevant to the query has changed. The selective recheck should assess the resolution, rather than equating identical listed identities with an automatically reusable typecheck.

The activity does not define the exact semantic comparison, so it would be premature to claim that any one stored field settles that question.
Does “selective” mean we recheck only queries whose old result was nonempty?

No; that would conflict with retaining empty-set records. Selectivity concerns which searches an edit can affect, not whether a search previously succeeded. An empty scoped query may be among the most important to revisit when a new candidate becomes relevant.

The reverse index needs to make those empty searches discoverable without requiring the compiler to recheck every cached declaration after every edit.
Are the three edit categories exhaustive for every possible reason to reconsider a typecheck?

The activity specifically names signature, visibility, and impl edits as triggers for these selective resolution rechecks. It does not state that no other change can affect typechecking, or that these query dependencies replace every other condition for safely reusing a declaration result.

Keeping the scope of the activity clear prevents this resolution mechanism from being mistaken for a complete account of all compiler dependencies.
How does the reverse index help with a candidate that did not exist when the query was recorded?

The link is to the *scoped search*, not to the future candidate’s identity. If an edit changes information that could alter that search, the reverse index must be able to find its recorded query. Rechecking can then discover what the edited program offers, even though the earlier result contained no such candidate.

That is also why storing empty-set queries is necessary: a prior lack of candidates must not make the search invisible to later edits.
Would it be accurate to describe TypeCache v2 as re-typechecking every declaration reached by the reverse index?

That would overstate this activity. It specifies **selective rechecks** of affected resolutions. Being reached by the reverse index means a cached query may need examination; it does not by itself establish that the entire declaration typecheck has to be discarded and repeated.

If a resolution’s relevant outcome changes, retaining its old cached typecheck unchanged would be unsafe. If the outcome does not change, the recheck may allow reuse, subject to the declaration’s other dependencies.
What would make an empty-set record ineffective despite storing it?

If the reverse index could not find that recorded search when an edit might populate it, the record would not protect the cached typecheck. Likewise, finding the query but failing to recheck its resolution would leave the old empty answer unexamined.

The three parts belong together: retain the query even when empty, connect relevant edits back to it, and recheck its resolution when those edits occur.
Can we specify the exact index layout or fingerprint fields from this activity?

Not from this activity alone. It commits to reverse-indexed scoped candidate queries, empty-set records, and selective rechecks after signature, visibility, or impl edits. It does not prescribe a storage layout, a fingerprint encoding, or a particular algorithm for comparing outcomes.

Those implementation choices would need to preserve the stated behavior: edits capable of changing a recorded resolution must reach it for rechecking, while unrelated cached searches need not be revisited.
What is the most concise description of the work item without claiming it is finished?

Implement TypeCache v2 so cached declaration typechecks retain reverse-indexed scoped candidate queries, including empty-set records, and selectively recheck affected resolutions after signature, visibility, or impl edits.

TypeCache v2 now records scoped positive and negative candidate queries and selectively rechecks declarations when indexed resolution outcomes change. What is the clearest way to describe this artifact?

Describe it in terms of what it records and what prompts declaration rechecks: **TypeCache v2 records scoped positive and negative candidate queries, then selectively rechecks declarations when indexed resolution outcomes change.** The queries express resolution facts on which a cached declaration typecheck depends. The scope identifies the context of the candidate search, and the positive and negative sides cover both candidates found and relevant absence or non-applicability.
What does “negative” mean in the description of something TypeCache v2 records?

It means a fact about a relevant candidate search that did *not* find an applicable alternative, or about an alternative that did not participate in the resolution. It does not necessarily mean that the compiler produced an error. A declaration can typecheck successfully while depending on a negative resolution fact.

Recording that query gives TypeCache v2 a dependency to reconsider if the search’s answer changes. It is different from recording only the candidate that was selected.
Why specify that the queries are scoped?

A candidate search has to be understood from the declaration’s resolution context. Candidates relevant in one scope need not be relevant in another. Calling the queries *scoped* makes clear that their answers are not treated as global facts solely about a name or trait goal.

The artifact description does not specify how scope is encoded. It identifies scope as part of the recorded resolution dependency.
Is it accurate to say TypeCache v2 stores both what resolution found and what the declaration relied on not finding?

Yes, as a conceptual explanation of positive and negative candidate queries. The positive side represents relevant candidate facts that resolution found; the negative side represents relevant absence or non-applicability facts. Both can matter to whether a cached declaration typecheck remains justified.

Keep the word *relevant* in that explanation. The description does not claim that TypeCache v2 stores every possible candidate or every fact about the program.
What does “indexed resolution outcomes change” mean here? Is any edit to the index enough?

No. The artifact says declarations are selectively rechecked **when indexed resolution outcomes change**. An edit that might affect a query and a change in its resolution outcome are distinct. The wording identifies the latter as the condition for selectively rechecking dependent declarations.

That distinction avoids describing TypeCache v2 as rechecking a declaration merely because some indexed information was touched. It also avoids assuming that a potentially relevant edit leaves resolution unchanged without examining its effect.
Does this say TypeCache v2 rechecks every cached declaration after a change?

No. “Selectively” limits the rechecks to declarations connected to changed indexed resolution outcomes. The artifact is not described as performing a blanket recheck of all cached declaration typechecks.

Nor does it imply that every recorded query changes after an edit. The relevant condition is a change in the indexed resolution outcome on which a declaration depends.
If a previously selected candidate remains present, why might a declaration still be rechecked?

Because the resolution outcome can depend on more than the continued presence of that candidate. A negative candidate query may cease to hold if another candidate becomes relevant. If that changes an indexed resolution outcome, TypeCache v2 selectively rechecks the dependent declaration even though its former candidate remains present.

The artifact description does not say what the recheck will conclude in a particular case. It says when the declaration is reconsidered.
Could a changed query lead to a new ambiguity?

It could. A newly relevant alternative is one way a resolution outcome might change, and ambiguity is a possible outcome under applicable resolution rules. The positive and negative query records are meant to make such changes visible to the dependency mechanism.

That is an explanation of why these dependencies matter, not a claim that this artifact description reports a particular ambiguity test or its result.
Is recording a negative candidate query the same as storing a list of rejected candidates?

Not necessarily. A negative query describes a relevant search and its resolution context; reducing it to a list of candidates that were already known would not, by itself, describe a candidate that appears later. The artifact states that TypeCache v2 records scoped negative *queries*, not merely lists of old candidate identities.

It does not specify the stored representation of each query, so the safest description stays at the query level.
Does the artifact say precisely how TypeCache v2 notices an outcome change?

No. It says that candidate queries are recorded and that declarations are selectively rechecked when indexed resolution outcomes change. It does not specify the index layout, the comparison procedure, or the exact representation of an outcome.

Those details should not be added to the artifact statement as though they were given here. The observable distinction in the statement is between recorded resolution dependencies and a change in their indexed outcomes.
Should I describe it as selectively rechecking queries or selectively rechecking declarations?

For this artifact, say **selectively rechecking declarations**. That is the action its description expressly names when indexed resolution outcomes change. You can explain that the recorded candidate queries identify resolution dependencies, but replacing “declarations” with “queries” would omit what the artifact says is rechecked in response to a changed outcome.
Does the description establish that every rechecked declaration gets a different typechecking result?

No. A changed indexed resolution outcome calls for reconsidering dependent declarations; it does not predetermine every result of that recheck. “Rechecks” describes work TypeCache v2 performs, not a guarantee that each declaration receives a different final diagnostic or typechecking result.
Can I say this artifact has already achieved clean-build parity and a particular reuse percentage?

Those are not claims made by this artifact description. Here the concrete facts are what TypeCache v2 records and when it selectively rechecks declarations. A statement about this artifact’s measured parity or reuse would need its own supporting result; it should not be inferred solely from the presence of the dependency mechanism.
Give me a concise wording that preserves all the important qualifiers.
“TypeCache v2 records scoped positive and negative candidate queries and selectively rechecks dependent declarations when indexed resolution outcomes change.”

The test is an activity to carry out, not an outcome. Its description supplies no parity result or reuse percentage.
Why put visibility, overload, and impl edits in the same test?

Each can change a resolution that a cached declaration depends on. Testing all three asks whether TypeCache v2 handles those kinds of changes without retaining an incorrect cached result or unnecessarily losing one whose dependencies remain unchanged.

That explains their relevance to the test; it does not predict how any individual edit will affect a resolution.
What is the clean-build comparison point for a given edit?

The diagnostic comparison matters directly: TypeCache v2 must not silently keep a cached successful resolution if the clean build reports ambiguity. When you say “unchanged-dependency reuse,” do you mean declarations whose source files were untouched?

What if an edit causes TypeCache v2 to inspect a candidate query, but the resolution outcome remains the same?

Could I calculate reuse as the fraction of all cached declarations kept after the edits?

That would be a different measure. The activity specifically calls for **unchanged-dependency reuse**. Does the name WorkspaceEdit-500 establish that this comparison covers exactly 500 edits?

Would matching diagnostics alone count as clean-build parity for this test?

Suppose an edit changes an indexed resolution outcome, but the declaration’s final diagnostic stays the same. Can the diagnostic comparison tell us everything?

The test records each of those observations for its own purpose.

How should cached trait proofs track transitive where-clause obligations when candidate heads remain unchanged across modules?

A candidate head remaining unchanged is not enough to establish that its cached proof remains valid. The head identifies a candidate that may match the goal; its where-clauses can impose further trait goals, and those goals can depend on information in other modules. A proof reused after an edit needs to remain justified all the way through those obligations, not merely at its first candidate match.

Conceptually, the cache should distinguish the candidate it considered from the resolution facts needed to discharge its obligations. The open design question is how to record those facts, including transitive ones, so a relevant cross-module change causes revalidation while an irrelevant edit does not discard the proof.
What makes an obligation transitive rather than just another condition on the candidate?

A direct where-clause obligation may itself require resolving a trait goal whose candidate has further where-clause obligations. Those further requirements are transitive dependencies of the original proof. Even if the original candidate head and its immediate where-clause text do not change, the outcome of a goal reached through that chain might change.

The distinction matters for caching because recording only the immediate obligation names would not necessarily establish that their own proofs remain justified after an edit.
Couldn’t I just cache the head and rerun its where-clauses whenever anything changes?

That would make the unchanged-head problem visible, but “anything changes” is much broader than the condition you want to detect. It could spend work on proofs whose obligation dependencies remain semantically unchanged. Conversely, checking only whether the head changed would miss edits that affect an obligation in another module.

The useful question is which resolution outcomes the proof relied on, directly or transitively, and whether an edit can change those outcomes. How to identify them precisely remains open here.
Suppose the original candidate still matches the trait goal exactly as before. Can its cached proof nevertheless be wrong?

Yes, in principle. Matching a candidate head and proving that candidate satisfies its where-clauses are different steps. If an obligation needed for the proof changes its outcome, the earlier proof may no longer justify the result despite an identical head. A clean resolution of the edited program must be the reference point.

That is the risk this question isolates: candidate-set tracking at the outer goal cannot, by itself, certify every transitive obligation used to establish applicability.
Does the dependency have to include only obligations that succeeded before the edit?

Not necessarily. A cached trait-resolution conclusion might rely on an obligation succeeding for one candidate and on another candidate’s obligations failing or otherwise not making it applicable. If an edit changes a relevant unsuccessful search, the overall resolution could change even while candidate heads stay fixed.

Which positive and negative facts must be retained depends on what justified the cached outcome. The requirement is to avoid treating a previously unsuccessful obligation as irrelevant if changing it could alter candidate applicability or the final resolution.
So a negative fact deep in a where-clause chain can matter too?

Yes, if that negative fact helps establish the resolution outcome being cached. Consider the general possibility that a candidate was not applicable because a nested obligation could not be satisfied. If an edit makes that obligation satisfiable, the candidate can become relevant without any change to its head. Whether it then changes the winner or creates ambiguity depends on the resolution rules.

A sound dependency account needs a way to notice that possibility; simply saving the old conclusion that the candidate was inapplicable would not be enough.
Is the answer to store the entire proof tree?

An entire proof tree is one conceivable representation of what was established, but storing it alone would not settle the invalidation question. The cache would still need to know which edits might change the meaning of facts used in that tree, including negative facts and facts arising in other modules. Conversely, a different representation might capture the necessary dependency information without preserving every proof step.

So I would treat “store the entire tree” as a possible design choice, not as a conclusion supplied by the question. The essential property is sound tracking of the resolution facts on which the proof depends.
Could I track only the immediate where-clause goals and let their own caches manage the rest?

That could be a way to organize dependencies if an outer proof cannot remain valid when any immediate goal’s relevant semantic outcome changes, and if each cached inner goal likewise tracks its own dependencies. The transitive guarantee would then come from following those links, rather than flattening every nested dependency into the outer record.

It is conditional: if an inner proof changes while its parent is not notified or revalidated, the outer proof can remain stale. The question is not whether dependencies must be stored flat or nested; it is whether changes propagate through the complete chain that justified the result.
What exactly should count as a changed inner goal outcome?

It has to be a semantic distinction that matters to the dependent proof. An inner goal changing from established to not established clearly matters. A change that makes an alternative applicable or introduces ambiguity may also matter under the language’s rules. On the other hand, an edit to information that leaves the relevant outcome equivalent need not automatically invalidate an outer proof on that ground.

Defining that equivalence precisely requires the trait-resolution semantics. Merely comparing an inner candidate’s head is too coarse for the situation you raised.
What if an inner proof finds a different route but reaches the same conclusion?

That is a useful test of the meaning of “unchanged.” If the alternative route is semantically equivalent for everything the outer proof relies on, the outer result might remain reusable on this dependency. But if the distinction affects applicability, diagnostics, or another fact the outer resolution needs, calling the outcomes identical would be unsafe.

The question does not specify an equality rule for proofs, so we should not assume either that every different route forces invalidation or that matching success alone always permits reuse.
How do module boundaries enter if none of the candidate heads changes?

An outer candidate can depend on where-clause goals whose resolutions draw on information outside its module. A change in that information can alter a nested obligation’s outcome without modifying the outer candidate head. The dependency has to lead from the edited information to the affected obligation and then to any cached proof that relies on it.

The module boundary is not a reason to stop tracking the chain. Nor does an edit in another module automatically mean every proof must be discarded; the relevant question is whether that proof’s transitive resolution dependencies can change.
Would fingerprints of candidate heads establish that the proof is reusable?

Not on their own. Even a perfectly unchanged head tells us only about the head. A where-clause obligation could resolve differently because of a separate cross-module edit. Whatever change-detection mechanism is used must account for facts that justify the nested proof, not merely identify changes to the outer candidate.

This is a conceptual limitation of head-only checking, not a claim that a particular fingerprint implementation has failed.
Could this problem also affect a cached failure to prove a trait goal?

Potentially. A cached failure can depend on the absence of an applicable proof route. If an edit changes a where-clause obligation along a previously unsuccessful route, that route may become viable while its candidate head remains unchanged. The cache therefore cannot regard failure as automatically stable simply because it previously found no successful candidate.

As with successful proofs, the precise dependencies are those needed to justify the cached resolution outcome, including any relevant negative searches.
If a nested obligation becomes satisfiable, must the outer result always change?

No. It makes the outer result worth reconsidering if that obligation belongs to a route relevant to the outer resolution. The final outcome might remain the same, or it might change; the answer depends on the other applicable candidates and the resolution rules. Detecting potential impact and concluding that the semantic outcome changed are distinct steps.

The tracking needs to be sound about the first step without assuming the second.
Would rechecking every outer declaration that mentions the trait be enough?

It could be a conservative response to some changes, but it does not express the desired dependency precision. An outer declaration might mention the same trait without relying on the changed obligation, while another proof might reach the changed obligation transitively in a less obvious way. A name-only connection does not by itself characterize either case.

The question calls for tracking which proofs actually depend on relevant obligation outcomes across modules, so rechecks can be directed appropriately without overlooking an indirect dependency.
How do we avoid losing the negative side when representing those transitive links?

For every conclusion used by an outer proof, ask not only which nested resolution succeeded but also which relevant alternatives were excluded and why the resolution could be considered settled. If an excluded route becomes applicable after an edit, its old exclusion may no longer support the cached outcome.

That does not prescribe a particular data structure or require recording every imaginable failure. It states the coverage condition: a negative fact that can affect the outer result must remain discoverable and recheckable even when it occurs several obligations deep.
So does this question imply that TypeCache v2 already handles transitive where-clause dependencies?

No. The question identifies a further soundness issue to examine for cached trait proofs. A description of scoped candidate queries does not, by itself, specify how dependencies propagate through nested where-clause obligations. We should not infer either that the existing mechanism handles them or that it fails; the tracking and revalidation requirements for these proofs still need to be made explicit.
What would be a good invariant to use while thinking about a representation?

A useful proposed invariant is: a cached trait-proof outcome may be reused only if the resolution facts that justify it—including relevant positive and negative outcomes of transitive where-clause obligations—remain semantically adequate for the edited program. If a cross-module edit can change one of those facts, the dependency mechanism must get the affected proof reconsidered, even if every candidate head on the outer search remains unchanged.

That states what a representation needs to support without asserting that a particular representation has been implemented or verified.

How can cached trait proofs record and revalidate the relevant positive and negative outcomes of *transitive where-clause obligations* across modules, so a change to those obligations is not missed when candidate heads stay unchanged, while semantically unchanged dependencies still permit reuse?

I propose extending TypeCache v2 with transitive trait-obligation dependencies, including failed proofs, and rechecking cached declarations when proof outcomes change. What exactly would that add to the cache’s reuse rule?

It would make a cached declaration depend not only on the trait candidate being considered, but also on the outcomes of the obligations needed to justify its trait resolution, including obligations reached through other obligations. A proof that failed can matter too: if its outcome changes, a previously inapplicable candidate might become relevant.

Under the proposal, a changed proof outcome prompts a recheck of cached declarations that depend on it. The proposal identifies the dependency and the response; it does not yet specify how the dependencies are represented or how changes are detected.
Why include failed proofs? Isn’t a cached trait proof just a record of what succeeded?

A resolution can rely on a candidate *not* qualifying as well as on another candidate qualifying. If the unsuccessful candidate was excluded because an obligation could not be proved, a later change to that failed proof could alter which candidates are applicable. Recording only successful proof paths could leave that relevant negative fact untracked.

“Including failed proofs” does not mean recording every unsuccessful proof attempt indiscriminately. It means that failures on which a cached resolution depends must be eligible for dependency tracking and reconsideration.
How is a transitive obligation different from the where-clause obligation immediately attached to a candidate?

An immediate obligation may itself be resolved using a proof with further obligations. Those further outcomes can be necessary to justify the original candidate’s applicability, even though they are not stated directly at the outer level. The proposed dependency has to follow that chain far enough that a change to a relevant inner outcome reaches the cached declaration.

“Transitive” describes that relationship. It does not require the outer cache entry to store every link in one flat list; it requires the dependency to remain effective through the chain.
Could the cache simply record the outer trait candidate and assume its obligations stay valid while that candidate remains present?

That assumption would not satisfy the proposed rule. A candidate remaining present says nothing by itself about whether an obligation required for its proof still has the same outcome. The new dependencies are intended to track those proof outcomes separately, including outcomes that arise across module boundaries.

The question for reuse becomes whether the proof facts justifying the cached declaration remain adequate, not merely whether the outer candidate is still available.
When you say “proof outcome,” are you referring only to success versus failure?

That is one essential distinction: a formerly successful obligation can fail, or a formerly failed one can succeed. But the outcome comparison must be as discriminating as the dependent resolution requires. If a changed proof would affect applicability, ambiguity, diagnostics, or executable behavior, the comparison must not treat the two outcomes as interchangeable.

The proposal does not fix a particular proof-outcome format or equivalence test. It calls for rechecking dependent declarations when the relevant outcome changes.
If an imported obligation changes internally but has the same relevant outcome, does the proposal demand a declaration recheck?

Not merely because its internal work differed. The stated trigger is a change in the *proof outcome* on which the cached declaration depends. An edit may make an obligation worth re-evaluating without ultimately changing that outcome.

That distinction matters for selective reuse: locating a potentially affected proof is not the same as finding a changed dependency. Of course, judging the outcomes equivalent must be sound for the declaration that relies on them.
Is a failed proof a dependency even if it was nowhere near the candidate ultimately selected?

Only if its failure is relevant to the cached resolution. The proposal includes failed proofs so a meaningful exclusion can be reconsidered when it changes; it does not assert that every failed goal encountered during typechecking must invalidate every declaration.

A useful test is whether changing that failure’s outcome could change the conclusion the declaration relies on. If so, leaving it out would make the dependency account incomplete. If not, it need not be treated as a dependency merely because it occurred during a search.
Suppose a failed inner obligation becomes provable. Does its outer declaration automatically get a different typechecking result?

Not automatically. A changed inner outcome makes an outer proof that depends on it—and ultimately a dependent cached declaration—subject to reconsideration. The final trait resolution might change, become ambiguous, or remain effectively the same after the applicable rules are run.

The proposal calls for a recheck when the proof outcome changes. It does not prejudge the result of that recheck.
What if a successful inner proof stops being provable instead?

That is the other direction the dependencies must cover. If a cached declaration relies on that successful proof through a chain of obligations, its cached result cannot simply keep using the former justification. A changed proof outcome should reach the dependent declaration for a recheck.

The rule is symmetric in this respect: both a failure becoming a success and a success becoming a failure can matter to trait resolution.
Does this mean a declaration must directly list every nested obligation it ultimately relies on?

Not necessarily. It could have a direct link to an obligation whose cached proof depends on another obligation, provided a change to the inner outcome propagates through those links to the declaration. Alternatively, a representation could make the transitive dependencies explicit at the declaration. The proposal does not choose between those organizations.

What it does require is that a relevant proof-outcome change cannot be stopped at an intermediate cache entry while an outer declaration continues to reuse an unjustified result.
If the impl head stays the same, would these dependencies still do any work?

Yes. The proposed trigger concerns proof outcomes, which can change independently of whether the outer candidate head changes. Tracking transitive obligations makes it possible to reconsider a cached declaration when the justification for using—or excluding—a candidate changes while the head remains stable.

That is a conceptual reason for adding proof dependencies, not a claim that a particular detection mechanism has already been implemented.
How would this relate to the positive and negative candidate queries TypeCache v2 already records?

They describe different facts that may justify a cached declaration. Candidate queries concern which candidates a resolution search can consider and relevant absences. Transitive trait-obligation dependencies concern whether the proofs needed for those candidates have the same outcomes. A candidate search and a proof of a candidate’s obligations can vary independently, so the proposed extension retains the candidate-query idea while adding proof-outcome dependencies.

A negative candidate fact and a failed proof are also distinct: the former concerns the search for candidates; the latter concerns an obligation that could affect whether a candidate qualifies.
Could a single changed inner proof affect more than one cached declaration?

Conceptually, yes. Several cached declarations might rely, directly or transitively, on the same proof outcome. The proposed rule would have each affected declaration rechecked when that outcome changes.

It does not require rechecking declarations that do not depend on that outcome. Nor does the proposal specify a data structure for finding the dependents.
What has to happen between detecting an edit and rechecking a declaration?

The compiler first has to determine which trait-obligation proofs the edit could affect and establish whether their relevant outcomes changed. A change then needs to reach proofs and declarations that depend on those outcomes, even through intermediate obligations. Only then can it selectively recheck the cached declarations implicated by the changed outcomes.

Those are logical obligations of the proposal, not a specified algorithm. An edit alone is a possible cause of a change; it is not itself proof that every dependent declaration’s outcome changed.
Would it be sound to compare only the outermost trait goal’s final success or failure?

That depends on whether the comparison preserves every distinction the cached declaration relies on. A final success or failure might be too coarse if a changed proof alters candidate applicability or produces a different resolution consequence without changing that simple label. The proposed transitive dependencies are meant to keep consequential changes visible through the proof chain.

The safe criterion is semantic adequacy for the dependent declaration, rather than a fixed assumption that a single Boolean at the outer goal captures all relevant proof changes.
Could tracking failed proofs make invalidation so broad that reuse becomes difficult?

It could if every failure were treated as a dependency of every nearby declaration, or if any potentially affected proof were equated with a changed outcome. The proposal instead names *transitive trait-obligation dependencies* and triggers declaration rechecks when the relevant proof outcomes change.

Precision would depend on identifying which failed proofs actually support a cached resolution and on distinguishing changed outcomes from edits that leave those outcomes equivalent. The proposal expresses that direction without claiming a measured reuse rate.
Does a changed proof outcome mean we must invalidate the declaration before rechecking it?

It means the cached declaration result cannot be accepted unchanged on the strength of its old proof dependency. The proposal’s stated action is to **recheck cached declarations** when proof outcomes change. That recheck establishes what the declaration means under the edited program; it need not imply that the final diagnostic or typechecking result will necessarily differ.

It is useful to keep a changed supporting proof distinct from the result of reconsidering the entire declaration.
How should this handle a failure nested several obligations deep in another module?

If that failure contributes to the outer resolution, it needs a dependency path back to the cached declaration, regardless of the module boundary or the number of intervening obligations. Should its relevant outcome change, the change must propagate along that path so the declaration is rechecked.

The proposal does not specify a maximum depth, a concrete proof graph, or a particular cross-module indexing scheme. The essential requirement is that transitive, relevant failed proofs are not dropped from the dependency account.
Am I proposing a fix that has already been shown to restore clean-build agreement?

No. You are proposing an extension to TypeCache v2: track transitive trait-obligation dependencies, include failed proofs, and recheck cached declarations when proof outcomes change. That describes what the cache should do; it is not a reported implementation or evaluation result.

The rationale is that a cached trait resolution can depend on proof outcomes beyond the outer candidate set. Whether this particular extension achieves the desired correctness and reuse properties would have to be established separately.
Give me a concise statement of the proposal that doesn’t accidentally say every edit forces a recheck.

Extend TypeCache v2 to track relevant transitive trait-obligation dependencies, including failed proofs, and selectively recheck cached declarations when those proof outcomes change—not merely whenever an edit occurs.
How can transitive proof dependencies capture failed and cyclic obligations without invalidating declarations for irrelevant impl edits?

The dependency needs to describe the resolution facts that justify a cached proof outcome, not just the impl head or the successful path. A failed obligation can be relevant because changing it might make a candidate applicable. A cyclic obligation can be relevant because its outcome may depend on how the cycle is resolved and on facts reached through it. The question is how to make those facts recheckable across the full dependency chain.

At the same time, an impl edit should prompt reconsideration only where it could affect a recorded obligation, and a potentially affected obligation should cause declaration invalidation only if its relevant semantic outcome changes. That separates finding possible impact from deciding that a cached result is no longer justified.
Why can’t we just record the obligations that eventually succeeded?

A failed obligation may explain why an alternative impl was not applicable. If an edit changes that failure into a success, the alternative may enter the resolution even though the previously successful proof is untouched. A dependency record containing only successful obligations would not necessarily notice that change.

The relevant failures are those whose outcomes contribute to the cached resolution. The question does not require retaining every failed attempt regardless of whether it could affect the declaration.
What is the special difficulty with a cyclic obligation?

A cycle means following dependencies may return to a goal already being considered. A representation that assumes every proof is a simple, finite chain of distinct goals could lose the relationship or expand it indefinitely. It also cannot simply label the cycle irrelevant: whether it affects the proof outcome depends on the trait-resolution rules.

The dependency account must preserve enough of that relationship to recognize a consequential change to facts involved in the cycle. This is a design obligation, not a claim that a particular cycle-handling strategy has been chosen.
Does encountering a cycle automatically mean the proof failed?

No general answer follows from the question. Different resolution semantics can treat cyclic obligations differently, so the cache should not substitute a universal “cycle means failure” rule for the compiler’s actual proof outcome. It needs to track whatever outcome the resolution produces, along with the dependencies relevant to keeping that outcome valid after an edit.
Could I store a link from each obligation to the obligation that called it?

Links between dependent obligations are one possible way to preserve transitivity: a change to an inner outcome could be propagated toward an outer proof and then its cached declaration. For cycles, those links would also have to represent a return to an obligation already in the dependency structure without pretending the relationship has ended.

Links alone would not answer which impl edits can change an obligation, or when an apparent internal change is semantically relevant. They address propagation, while edit-to-obligation matching and outcome comparison remain separate questions.
How should a failed proof be represented if there was no impl that worked?

It can be understood as a recorded negative resolution outcome for a particular obligation in its relevant context, rather than as a reference to a successful impl. Its dependency must remain sensitive to an edit that could make a proof route viable. Otherwise an absence of a successful impl would also mean an absence of any way to revisit the cached failure.

The exact representation is open. The important property is that a relevant newly viable impl can reach that failed obligation for revalidation.
But if we associate every failed goal with every impl edit, won’t we destroy reuse?

That would be unnecessarily broad if the compiler can determine that many edits cannot affect the goal. The intended distinction is between an impl edit that *might* change a failed obligation’s proof outcome and one that cannot. Even among potentially affecting edits, revalidation may find that the outcome is semantically unchanged.

This leaves two precision questions: how to identify the obligations an edit could affect without omissions, and how to avoid propagating invalidation when the relevant outcomes remain the same. Soundness prevents ignoring a possible change; it does not require treating every impl edit as consequential.
Does an impl edit have to change the candidate set to matter to one of these proof dependencies?

Not necessarily. An obligation’s proof can depend on further obligations, so the same outer candidate may remain present while the justification for using it changes. A dependency scheme concerned only with whether the outer candidate set changed would not express every potential change to a transitive proof outcome.

For this question, the key is to follow the proof dependencies relevant to the declaration, including failures and cycles, and check whether an impl edit can change their outcomes. Candidate-set information may help locate work, but it is not a complete description of an obligation’s proof.
When should a change to an inner failed obligation reach an outer declaration?

When the outer declaration’s cached resolution depends, directly or transitively, on that failure. A change in the inner outcome needs to travel through the intervening proof dependencies to the declaration so its cached typecheck can be reconsidered. If the failed obligation played no role in justifying the outer outcome, merely encountering it somewhere during resolution would not automatically make the declaration dependent on it.

The unresolved part is how to identify those relevant paths precisely, especially where the dependency structure contains cycles.
What if an edit changes a goal inside a cycle but the cycle’s resolved outcome stays the same?

The edit may justify re-evaluating that part of the proof, but it need not justify invalidating every declaration reachable from the cycle. If the relevant outcome for the enclosing proof remains semantically equivalent, propagation can stop on that basis—provided the equivalence judgment is sound under the compiler’s resolution rules.

The question therefore calls for more than recording that a cycle exists. It calls for a way to detect possible impact and then compare the proof outcomes that outer declarations actually rely on.
Could we represent a cycle as one combined dependency instead of expanding every path through it?

That is a possible conceptual approach to examine. It might avoid repeatedly traversing the same obligation relationships, provided it preserves every edit that could affect the combined outcome and makes changes visible to dependents outside the cycle. It would still have to respect the language’s meaning for cyclic proofs and failures.

The question does not choose a combined representation or establish that it would be sufficiently precise. The standard for any representation is whether it catches relevant outcome changes without invalidating declarations for unrelated impl edits.
Is a changed failed proof always enough to say the outer declaration’s final resolution changed?

No. A failed proof becoming successful can change which routes are available, but the enclosing resolution might still yield the same relevant semantic result. It should trigger reconsideration along dependency paths where that failure mattered; the reconsideration determines whether the outcome relied on by a cached declaration has actually changed.

Conflating a changed inner proof with a changed final declaration would cause avoidable invalidation. Ignoring the changed inner proof could miss a newly applicable candidate or an ambiguity.
How would you distinguish an irrelevant impl edit from one that merely turns out harmless after a recheck?

An irrelevant edit can be ruled out as unable to affect the obligation’s relevant proof search, so that obligation need not be revalidated on its account. A potentially relevant edit may reach the obligation and require revalidation, yet prove harmless because its semantic outcome remains unchanged. Neither case should invalidate dependent declarations solely because an impl was edited.

The first distinction depends on sound edit-to-obligation matching; the second depends on sound comparison of proof outcomes. The question asks for both coverage and precision, without prescribing either mechanism.
Does the comparison need to distinguish a failed proof from an ambiguous proof outcome?

If the trait-resolution semantics distinguish those outcomes in ways that matter to the dependent declaration, then yes. A comparison that reduces every non-success to the same value could miss a change relevant to diagnostics or applicability. Likewise, success cannot be presumed equivalent just because the outer impl head is unchanged.

The appropriate equality notion is semantic: it must preserve the distinctions on which reuse, diagnostics, and executable behavior depend. This question does not specify the language’s complete set of proof outcomes.
Can I phrase the requirement as tracking every obligation visited during resolution?

That might record more than the result depends on and invite invalidation from irrelevant impl edits. The more precise requirement is to track the positive and negative proof outcomes that justify the cached resolution, including those reached transitively and those involved in cycles. A visited obligation is a possible dependency, but its mere presence during a search does not establish that every change to it must invalidate the declaration.

The design still has to be conservative wherever it cannot safely determine relevance. Precision cannot come at the cost of missing an obligation whose changed outcome could affect the result.
What invariant could guide a design for these dependencies?

A useful proposed invariant is: a cached declaration may continue to rely on a trait proof only if every relevant transitive obligation outcome—including failed outcomes and outcomes involving cycles—remains semantically adequate for that proof. An impl edit that could change one of those outcomes must make it eligible for revalidation; an edit that cannot affect them should not force declaration invalidation.

Where revalidation establishes no relevant outcome change, the edit alone gives no reason on that dependency to discard the declaration’s typechecking result. This is a criterion to design for, not a statement that an implementation has met it.
So the difficult part isn’t merely remembering that a failure or cycle happened?

Right. The cache needs to know which failed or cyclic obligation outcomes actually support a cached resolution, how a potentially consequential impl edit reaches those obligations, and how a changed outcome propagates through transitive dependencies to a declaration. It also needs to stop treating an edit as consequential when revalidation shows the relevant outcome is unchanged.

Simply recording a failure or a cycle without those relationships would not answer when a declaration must be reconsidered—or when it can safely be left alone.

Here’s a hypothesis: canonical obligation proof DAGs with SCC and failed-goal dependencies should eliminate the TransitiveWhere-200 mismatches while preserving at least 95% unchanged-dependency reuse. Does that address both failed and cyclic obligations?

That is the intended coverage, but it remains a hypothesis. A proof dependency structure could make the obligations supporting a cached trait result explicit, including goals reached transitively. Failed-goal dependencies would retain relevant unsuccessful proof outcomes, while SCCs—strongly connected components—would represent mutually dependent obligations where a simple chain cannot describe a cycle.

The proposed result has two parts that would need separate evaluation: no TransitiveWhere-200 diagnostic or behavioral mismatches against clean builds, and at least 95% reuse of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. Specifying the structure does not yet demonstrate either result.
Why call it a proof DAG if cyclic obligations are part of the problem?

The distinction is between the underlying obligation relationships, which may contain cycles, and a representation that groups a cycle into a strongly connected component. The relationships between those components can then be viewed as a directed acyclic graph, or DAG. That gives the hypothesis a way to retain cyclic dependencies without pretending every proof is a linear chain or following a cycle indefinitely.

The grouping must still preserve whatever proof outcome the compiler’s trait-resolution rules assign to the cycle. Calling the representation a DAG is not a claim that the obligations themselves are cycle-free.
What does “canonical” need to achieve here?

It should let the dependency structure recognize obligations as the same relevant goal when differences in their presentation do not change their meaning. That could make it possible to associate cached proofs and edits with the obligations they actually affect, even when those obligations appear at different points in a transitive proof.

Canonicalization must not erase context that affects proof outcomes. If two goals are grouped as equivalent when their resolution-relevant circumstances differ, a change could be missed. The hypothesis names a canonical structure; it does not specify or validate a canonicalization rule.
How would the failed-goal part protect an impl that was previously ruled out?

If an impl’s applicability depended on an obligation that failed, that failure can be part of the reason the cached resolution excluded the impl. A failed-goal dependency would keep that negative proof outcome connected to the cached result. If an edit could make the goal provable, the goal could be reconsidered even though the impl head itself was unchanged.

A changed inner outcome would then need to reach the dependent resolution. Whether the impl ultimately becomes applicable, changes the selected result, or creates an ambiguity is for resolution under the edited program to determine; the dependency alone does not decide it.
Does the hypothesis require storing every failed goal the solver ever visits?

No. It calls for failed-goal *dependencies*: failures relevant to justifying a cached proof or resolution outcome. A failed attempt that could not affect that outcome need not automatically become a reason to invalidate its declaration.

This distinction matters to the reuse part of the hypothesis. If unrelated impl edits trigger invalidation through failures that were never consequential, the structure might be safe but fail to preserve at least 95% unchanged-dependency reuse.
What if the relevant failure is inside a cycle rather than on a straightforward proof branch?

The proposed structure needs to retain both relationships: the failure as a relevant outcome and its place within the cyclic dependency represented by an SCC. If an edit can change that outcome, re-evaluation must be able to affect the component’s relevant proof result and, where necessary, proofs depending on the component.

The SCC label is not itself an answer to whether the failure can become a success or how the cycle resolves. Those questions still depend on the compiler’s trait-resolution semantics. The hypothesis is that representing the relationships will allow consequential changes to be found and propagated.
Could an SCC make invalidation too broad by tying every goal in a cycle together?

That is a precision concern worth testing. Goals in an SCC are mutually dependent, so a potentially relevant edit may require reconsidering the component. But that need not mean every declaration depending on the component loses its cached typecheck. The component’s relevant semantic outcome can be compared after reconsideration, and an unchanged outcome need not propagate invalidation on that ground.

If the representation cannot distinguish an edit that affects the component from one that cannot, or treats every inspection as a changed outcome, reuse could suffer. The at-least-95% condition is part of the hypothesis precisely so correctness is not the only consideration.
Why would this structure help when the outer candidate set is unchanged?

The proposed dependencies reach into the proof obligations that justify a candidate’s applicability. A candidate set can remain identical while an imported obligation’s proof outcome changes. A canonical obligation structure with links through transitive goals would give the cached declaration a dependency on that outcome, rather than assuming stable candidates imply stable proofs.

That explains why the hypothesis is relevant to the TransitiveWhere-200 mismatches. It does not establish that a particular proof DAG has already captured every consequential imported obligation.
Does it matter whether an obligation changes from success to failure or from failure to success?

Both directions can matter. Losing a proof can undermine a candidate that previously qualified; gaining a proof can make a previously excluded candidate relevant. The failed-goal dependency is particularly important for the second direction, while the proof structure also has to preserve the dependencies of successful outcomes.

Neither direction automatically determines the outer declaration’s final result. The hypothesis depends on finding a changed relevant proof outcome and reconsidering its dependents, then comparing the edited resolution with what a clean build would produce.
Is an edit to any impl mentioned in the proof DAG sufficient reason to discard the cached declaration?

No. A possible impact on a goal, a changed goal outcome, and a changed declaration result are different things. The proposed dependency structure should make an impl edit reach goals it could affect, but the goal’s relevant outcome may remain unchanged. Even if an inner outcome changes, the effect on an outer proof needs to be evaluated rather than presumed.

The hypothesis combines coverage with selectivity: it aims to eliminate the named mismatches without invalidating declarations merely because an impl edit occurred somewhere in a related search.
How should we understand the ≥95% threshold in this hypothesis?

It means reuse of at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. It is not a requirement to reuse 95% of every declaration after every edit, and it would not justify retaining a cached result whose relevant proof outcome has changed.

The proof DAG, SCC, and failed-goal dependencies are hypothesized to track changes precisely enough to retain eligible results. No reuse measurement for this proposed structure is stated here.
Could a different internal proof route count as an unchanged dependency?

Possibly, if the difference leaves every semantic outcome relevant to the cached declaration equivalent. Treating all different routes as changed could reduce reuse. But treating all proofs with the same superficial success label as equivalent could miss a change that affects applicability or diagnostics.

The hypothesis needs a sound notion of proof-outcome equivalence. “Canonical” may help identify and compare obligations, but it does not, by itself, define which proof changes can be ignored.
What would count as eliminating the TransitiveWhere-200 mismatches?

For the edited programs in TransitiveWhere-200, the cached compiler would need to match the corresponding clean builds on the diagnostic and executable-behavior comparisons. A proof DAG that merely notices edits would not suffice if stale diagnostics or behavior differences remained.

That is the outcome predicted by the hypothesis, not an observed result for this proposed extension. Likewise, achieving parity on that test would not alone establish the separate reuse threshold.
Does that prediction commit us to a particular algorithm for constructing SCCs or indexing edits?

No. The hypothesis identifies canonical obligation proof DAGs with SCC and failed-goal dependencies as the proposed representation and predicts two outcomes. It does not specify an SCC algorithm, a storage layout, or an edit index.

Whatever implementation is considered would have to find edits capable of changing relevant goals, preserve dependencies through cycles, and distinguish unchanged from changed semantic proof outcomes. Those are conditions for evaluating the hypothesis, not additional implementation decisions already made.
What if the proof structure catches every change but reuse falls below 95%?

Then it would not satisfy the hypothesis as stated. Eliminating the TransitiveWhere-200 mismatches addresses its correctness prediction; preserving at least 95% unchanged-dependency reuse is a separate prediction. A broad invalidation strategy could meet the first while missing the second.

Conversely, high reuse would not compensate for any diagnostic or executable-behavior mismatch. Both parts must be assessed on their own terms.
And what if the reuse target is met but a cyclic obligation still leaves a stale diagnostic?

That would fail the predicted mismatch-elimination result. A cached declaration whose relevant cyclic proof outcome has changed cannot be kept merely to preserve reuse. The SCC portion is proposed to make such dependencies representable and recheckable, not to relax clean-build agreement.

The hypothesis remains unconfirmed until the behavior of the proposed structure is evaluated. An appealing representation and a reuse prediction do not themselves establish correctness.

Can you explain the DAG and SCC combination without assuming that trait proofs never contain cycles?

Thus the DAG description does not mean the underlying obligations are cycle-free.

What does the failed-goal index add?

It gives a relevant unsuccessful proof outcome a route back into consideration after an edit. A cached resolution may rely on an obligation’s failure to exclude a candidate. If that goal could become provable, the earlier failure cannot simply remain an unexamined fact.

The index should identify failed goals that an edit might affect. That is different from saying that every failed goal changes, or that every edit concerning an impl must invalidate every declaration.
Are we indexing all failed proof attempts, including ones that did not affect a cached declaration?

The stated activity calls for *failed-goal indexes*, but it does not define their membership rule. The purpose is to make relevant failed-goal dependencies discoverable. Indexing failures that cannot affect a cached outcome could add work without improving correctness; omitting failures that do justify an outcome could miss a consequential change.

That balance is one of the things the implementation needs to handle. We should not present a particular indexing rule as already specified.
And what is “canonical” supposed to accomplish in this work item?

Canonicalization must preserve distinctions that affect resolution. The work item does not specify the canonical form, so it would be premature to claim that any particular normalization or equality test is sufficient.
If an edit touches an impl connected to a failed goal, do we immediately recheck every declaration depending on that goal?

Not necessarily. There is a difference between an edit that *could* affect an indexed failed goal and a change in that goal’s relevant proof outcome. That distinction matters for the reuse measurement. Potential impact should not automatically be counted as a lost declaration typecheck when the semantic dependencies remain unchanged.
How should a changed goal inside an SCC reach a declaration outside the cycle?

The representation needs dependency links from the affected obligation through its SCC and onward to any enclosing proof that relies on the component. Could we evaluate parity just by checking that the new index visits the right goals?

Internal observations can help explain a result, but they do not replace the clean-build comparison.
What exactly should unchanged-dependency reuse measure in this test?

It should measure reuse of cached typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. The activity calls for testing that reuse alongside parity. It does not report a reuse figure.
Does testing TransitiveWhere-200 alone tell us how the extension handles every cyclic trait proof?

No. TransitiveWhere-200 is the named evaluation for this activity, while the SCC addition addresses cyclic obligation dependencies in the implementation.
