I’d like to propose validating per-declaration resolution certificates against edited interface summaries. The certificates should cover candidate absence, alias normalization, and coherence witnesses. What is the basic reuse rule?

For each cached declaration typecheck, retain a certificate describing the resolution facts needed to justify it. After an edit, validate that certificate against summaries of the edited interfaces. Reuse the typecheck on this basis only if validation establishes that the relevant facts still hold.

The three named kinds of evidence matter for different reasons: candidate absence accounts for relevant alternatives that were not available or applicable, alias normalization accounts for the question being resolved, and coherence witnesses account for facts affecting how candidates resolve. This is a proposed rule, not a claim that a certificate format or validator has been implemented.
What does ‘per-declaration’ add to the proposal?

It makes the declaration typecheck the unit whose reuse is being justified. Different declarations can depend on different resolution questions, so each certificate should speak to the facts relevant to its own cached result. An edit to an interface might affect one declaration’s certificate and leave another’s valid.

That does not prescribe how certificates are stored or whether they share underlying information. It identifies the scope of the proposed validation and reuse decision.
Is a resolution certificate just a record of the overload or impl that was selected?

No. Recording the selected candidate alone would not justify why the result remains correct after an edit. A new alternative could become relevant while the old selection remains present. The proposal expressly includes candidate absence, as well as alias normalization and coherence witnesses, because the result can rely on facts beyond the identity of its former winner.

A certificate is meant to carry the relevant justification for resolution. The proposal does not specify its exact contents or encoding.
Why validate against *edited* interface summaries?

The edited interfaces describe the cross-module information available to resolution after the edit. Checking a certificate only against the information from the earlier build would confirm a fact about the old program, not whether the declaration’s cached resolution remains justified in the new one.

The summaries have to convey enough information for the validation they support. The word ‘summary’ does not, by itself, guarantee that all relevant changes are represented.
What would candidate absence mean when a declaration already had a successful resolution?

A successful resolution can rely on a relevant alternative *not* participating. Candidate absence could certify that a search from this declaration’s context found no additional candidate capable of changing its resolution. After an edit, validation would need to consider whether that absence still holds.

It need not mean that no candidates of any kind exist, and it does not necessarily represent a user-facing error. The absent alternatives must be defined relative to the declaration’s actual resolution question.
How could a certificate describe a candidate that did not exist when it was created?

It cannot name the identity of a future candidate. Instead, an absence claim has to describe the relevant search condition whose truth could change when one appears. Validating that claim against edited interface summaries can then detect whether the edited program supplies a consequential alternative.

That is an obligation for the proposed certificate and summary design. A record containing only previously encountered candidate identities would not, by itself, establish continued absence.
If a new candidate appears somewhere else but cannot participate in this declaration’s resolution, should validation fail?

Not simply because a candidate was added elsewhere. Validation should concern the absence claim relevant to this declaration. An edit could make that claim worth checking without making it false. If the edited summaries establish that the declaration’s relevant resolution facts still hold, that addition alone would not defeat reuse on this ground.

The difficulty is making the absence claim and its scope both sound and precise; the proposal does not say a particular representation already achieves that.
Could candidate absence also matter for a trait implementation that used to be inapplicable?

Yes, if its inapplicability is a relevant reason the cached resolution was justified. An edit may make a previously excluded route viable without removing the candidate that was formerly selected. A certificate that relies on the exclusion must make that fact subject to validation.

The proposal names candidate absence; it does not define a complete classification of all trait-proof outcomes or prescribe how an inapplicable implementation is represented.
What exactly is the alias-normalization part certifying?

It concerns how an alias-dependent resolution question is formed. An upstream edit could change the normalized form of a type or trait goal while the declaration’s own text remains unchanged. A certificate that only preserves the earlier, fully formed goal might validate an answer to a question the edited declaration no longer asks.

Alias-normalization evidence should therefore make the relevant formation of the resolution question checkable against the edited interface summaries. The proposal does not specify a normalization algorithm or an equality rule for normalized forms.
If the old and new normalized goals look identical, is that enough to reuse the typecheck?

Not by itself. That comparison could establish that this part of goal formation remains the same, if the comparison is sound. The candidates, their proofs, coherence-relevant facts, and any other dependencies of the cached typecheck must still be justified.

A certificate needs validation as a whole. Matching one alias-normalization fact is not a certificate for every resolution outcome the declaration relies on.
What if an alias edit changes the normalized goal but the final declaration-level result happens to look the same?

The earlier answer cannot simply be treated as an answer to the newly formed goal. The edited question must be considered before deciding whether the relevant semantic resolution outcome remains equivalent. A changed normalized goal does not by itself predict a different final diagnostic or executable behavior, but it does defeat an unchecked assumption that the old question still applies.

The proposal leaves open how the validator handles that case. It does not authorize reuse on the strength of a superficial resemblance between final results.
What is a coherence witness supposed to contribute?

It is intended to make a coherence-relevant part of the resolution justification checkable. Candidate identities and proof results alone may not establish that the edited program resolves an alternative in the same way; coherence information can matter to whether a resolution is unique or ambiguous. A witness would provide evidence for the relevant coherence condition that the certificate relies on.

‘Coherence witness’ names the kind of evidence proposed. It does not specify a concrete witness structure or a particular language’s coherence rules.
Would a witness that merely says ‘not ambiguous last time’ be sufficient?

Not on its own. That reports the earlier conclusion without explaining why the conclusion should survive an edit. Validation needs a coherence-relevant fact that can be checked against the edited summaries, including when a newly relevant alternative changes the result.

The exact fact depends on the resolver’s semantics. The soundness requirement is that a newly ambiguous edited resolution cannot be certified as unchanged merely because the earlier result was unambiguous.
Do coherence witnesses replace candidate-absence claims?

No. They address related but distinct parts of the justification. Candidate absence concerns whether relevant alternatives participate in the declaration’s search. A coherence witness concerns the resolution-relevant relationships or conditions among alternatives. An edit might affect either, and checking one does not automatically establish the other.

The proposal includes both rather than treating them as interchangeable.
Could a coherence witness remain valid while candidate absence becomes false?

Conceptually, yes. The witness might still describe the facts it was meant to establish, while the edited interfaces introduce another relevant candidate. The certificate would then need to address that new candidate before the declaration’s earlier resolution could be reused. Validation of one certificate component is not enough when another relevant component no longer holds.
And could the candidate set remain the same while a coherence witness fails validation?

That is also possible in principle. An unchanged set of candidate identities does not necessarily establish unchanged coherence-relevant resolution facts. If a witness on which the cached result relies fails against the edited summaries, candidate-set stability alone cannot justify retaining the old resolution.

Neither possibility asserts that a particular edit has produced that result; they explain why the proposal calls for distinct kinds of certificate evidence.
How would this approach deal with an edit that makes a call ambiguous?

Validation must not certify the cached unambiguous outcome if the edited interface information makes ambiguity relevant to that declaration. A changed candidate-absence fact, a changed coherence-relevant fact, or another relevant certificate condition could require the resolution to be reconsidered. The resulting incremental diagnostics must ultimately reflect the edited program as a clean build would.

The proposal does not specify which certificate component would detect every possible ambiguity. That coverage would have to be established for the resolution rules in question.
Is a failed certificate the same as proof that the final typecheck must differ?

No. Failure to validate says the certificate no longer justifies retaining the cached result *without further consideration*. The declaration might ultimately typecheck the same way after being reconsidered, or it might not. A failed check of the earlier justification and a changed final result are different conclusions.

The proposal does not specify the work done after validation fails. It specifies the condition under which the existing certificate can support reuse.
Could a summary change textually while its relevant certificate facts remain valid?

Yes. The point of validation is to assess the resolution facts that matter to this declaration, rather than treat any interface edit as automatic declaration invalidation. An edited summary could differ while still satisfying a particular certificate’s candidate-absence, alias-normalization, and coherence conditions.

That precision is useful only if validation is sound. Treating a consequential semantic change as irrelevant would incorrectly retain a cached typecheck.
Does the proposal tell us how the validator finds certificates affected by an interface edit?

No. It says to validate per-declaration resolution certificates against edited interface summaries, but it does not prescribe an index, lookup rule, or validation schedule. An implementation would need a sound way to avoid trusting a certificate whose relevant interface facts might have changed.

That is a distinct question from what the certificate says once it has been selected for validation.
Could we validate only certificates that mention an edited candidate by identity?

That would not generally cover a candidate-absence claim: a newly introduced candidate had no identity in the earlier certificate. It might also miss a change to information used for alias normalization or a coherence witness. A sound selection rule must account for edits that could falsify the certificate’s relevant claims, not only edits to entities it explicitly names as prior candidates.

This is a conceptual limitation of identity-only lookup, not a claim about a validator already built.
How complete must the edited interface summaries be?

Complete enough for the claims being validated. If a relevant candidate addition, alias-normalization change, or coherence change is omitted from the summaries, apparent certificate validity would not establish that the edited program has the same resolution outcome. Conversely, summaries need not be described as copies of entire modules simply because these facts must be checkable.

The proposal gives no summary schema. Its soundness depends on the summaries and certificates together covering the facts required for reuse.
Does validating a resolution certificate establish that every part of a declaration’s typecheck can be reused?

It establishes only what the certificate soundly covers. The proposal is about resolution dependencies of a declaration typecheck. If some other information needed by typechecking has changed, validating the resolution certificate alone would not make the entire cached result safe to retain.

The proposed reuse decision must therefore be read as conditional on the certificate being adequate for the resolution facts it represents and on other required grounds for reuse still holding.
Would the certificates have to include transitive proof information?

They would need to cover any transitive proof outcomes that are relevant to the declaration’s resolution; otherwise validating only an outer candidate could miss a changed obligation that affects applicability. The proposal itself names candidate absence, alias normalization, and coherence witnesses, but does not prescribe a complete proof representation or say how such dependencies are encoded.

That is a completeness question for the certificate design, not a reported feature of an implementation.
Could certificate validation replace replaying the entire resolution question?

That is a possible aim, but the proposal does not guarantee it. If edited summaries can establish that all relevant certificate claims still hold, reuse may be justified without fully re-solving a declaration’s resolution. If they cannot, some resolution work may be required. The proposal specifies validating certificates, not an absolute rule that replay is never needed.

No cost comparison between validation and replay is given here.
What would make a certificate too coarse for the clean-build requirement?

One that treats semantically different outcomes as equivalent. For example, it cannot ignore a newly relevant candidate or treat an ambiguous resolution as interchangeable with a previously unique one. It also cannot assume that the old canonical trait goal is still the right question after a consequential alias change, or that coherence facts remain valid without checking them.

The standard is whether accepting the certificate preserves the diagnostics and executable behavior a clean build of the edited program would produce. The proposal has not yet shown that any particular certificate meets that standard.
Could certificates be too sensitive and invalidate results unnecessarily?

Yes. If validation fails merely because an interface summary changed textually, even when every resolution fact relevant to a declaration remains semantically unchanged, the cache may lose reusable typechecking results. The certificate should be specific enough to distinguish a changed justification from an edit that leaves that justification intact.

That is the precision side of the design problem. It must not be obtained by making the certificate so coarse that it misses a consequential change.
How does this proposal relate to the at-least-95% reuse target?

Per-declaration validation offers a possible way to retain typechecking results when their resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged, even after edits elsewhere. The target is to reuse at least 95% of typechecking results for that eligible class while maintaining clean-build diagnostics and executable behavior.

The certificate proposal contains no reuse measurement or parity result. It suggests a mechanism that would need to satisfy both requirements; it does not establish that it already does.
If a certificate validates for candidate absence and aliases but not coherence, may we count that typecheck as reused to reach 95%?

Not on the strength of that incomplete validation. If a coherence witness relevant to the cached outcome no longer validates, the certificate as a whole does not justify retaining the typecheck unchanged. Counting unjustified retention would not be sound reuse, regardless of the percentage.

Further consideration might establish an equivalent outcome, but that would require evidence beyond the failed coherence check.
Does ‘witness’ mean we have already proved coherence across all future edits?

No. A witness is proposed as evidence to be *validated* against the edited interface summaries. It cannot be treated as permanently valid just because it justified an earlier resolution. The proposal also does not claim that a witness for one declaration says anything about every other declaration or future edit.
What is the most useful separation of stages in this approach?

First, associate a cached declaration with a certificate of its relevant resolution facts. Second, use the edited interface summaries to assess whether those facts—including candidate absence, alias normalization, and coherence witnesses—still hold. Third, decide whether the cached typecheck may be retained on that resolution basis, respecting any other typechecking dependencies.

Producing a certificate, validating it, and retaining the declaration result are distinct actions. The proposal identifies them conceptually without specifying an implementation or reporting an evaluation.
Can you give me a compact statement of the proposal, keeping its status clear?

Propose per-declaration resolution certificates covering candidate absence, alias normalization, and coherence witnesses; validate them against edited interface summaries before reusing cached typechecks. Whether this provides clean-build parity and at least 95% unchanged-dependency reuse remains to be established.
How can resolution certificates prove candidate absence across wildcard reexports without rescanning every imported module after an edit?

The certificate cannot merely list the candidates found when the declaration was checked. An absence claim must cover the declaration’s relevant search through wildcard reexports, including paths that yielded no candidate at the time. Otherwise an edit could make a candidate visible along one of those paths without changing anything named in the old certificate.

The design question is how to validate that absence against edited interface information selectively. It needs enough information to establish that each relevant reexport path still contributes no candidate that would affect the resolution, while avoiding a fresh scan of every imported module for every edit. That is a requirement for a possible certificate design, not a demonstrated mechanism.
Why are wildcard reexports harder than recording a dependency on a named imported candidate?

A named candidate already found can be recorded as an existing dependency. A wildcard reexport also creates a route by which a candidate not previously found could become visible. The earlier typecheck cannot record the identity of that future candidate, so a certificate of absence must refer to the relevant search through the reexport, not just to identities in the earlier candidate set.

The difficulty is maintaining a useful negative claim as imported interfaces change. Checking only that previously found candidates are unchanged would not establish continued absence.
Does the certificate need to say that every imported module contains no candidates at all?

No. Its claim should be about candidates relevant to this declaration’s resolution and visibility context. An imported module may contain other declarations without affecting the claim. Proving the broader statement that every module contains no candidates would be both unnecessary and potentially false.

What counts as relevant depends on the resolution rules. The certificate must be narrow enough to support selective validation, but not so narrow that it overlooks a newly visible overload or trait candidate.
Could I just record ‘this name was absent’ at the declaration’s scope?

That describes the earlier result, but not yet why it remains true after an edit. For an absence certificate to be useful, the edited interface information must let the validator check the relevant wildcard-reexport routes that contribute to that scoped name search. If the record merely repeats the old answer, it could validate itself while the search has changed.

A scoped absence claim is a sensible question to represent. The unresolved part is what evidence lets it be revalidated without rescanning every imported module.
What if a reexported module adds a declaration with the relevant name?

That is a change an absence certificate must be able to notice when the new declaration can participate in the scoped resolution. A route that previously contributed no relevant candidate may now contribute one. The certificate’s old negative result would then need reconsideration; the final resolution might change or might remain equivalent after applicability and other rules are considered.

The change should not be missed merely because the newly added declaration had no identity in the earlier cache. Nor does the addition alone prove that the cached declaration’s final typecheck must change.
And if the added declaration cannot be seen through the wildcard reexport from this scope?

Then it should not be treated as a newly visible candidate for this declaration. The certificate concerns the search as resolved from its scope, so visibility through the reexport path matters. An edit can be worth examining while validation still establishes that the relevant absence claim holds.

The design must distinguish that harmless case from an addition that actually reaches the declaration. The question does not specify a particular language’s visibility rules or how to summarize them.
Could a wildcard reexport change while the module providing the candidate remains untouched?

Conceptually, yes. The relevant search depends not only on candidate declarations but also on whether a reexport path makes them visible from the declaration’s context. A change to that path can alter the scope-qualified candidate search without modifying the candidate itself.

A sound absence certificate must therefore be sensitive to changes in relevant visibility relationships, not only to additions or edits within the modules that contain candidates.
What does ‘without rescanning every imported module’ actually require? Can we avoid all work on import edits?

It does not mean doing no work. It asks whether edited interface information can direct validation to the relevant portions of a search and provide enough evidence that other portions have not changed in a consequential way. Some rechecking may be necessary when a relevant wildcard path or its contents change.

Avoiding *every* scan is different from avoiding a blanket scan of *every imported module* after each edit. The latter is the concern expressed in the question; the former would be a stronger promise not stated here.
Would a summary of what names each wildcard path can expose help?

That is one conceptual possibility to examine. A summary could help determine whether an edit can affect a certificate’s relevant name search, including a search that previously returned no candidate. To support a proof of absence, the summary would have to account for the visibility context and remain current when either the reexport path or reachable interface information changes.

Merely having a summary would not prove correctness: if it omits a consequential addition or visibility change, validation could accept a stale certificate. The question has not selected a summary format or established that one avoids all necessary rescanning.
If a summary says a name is absent, why not trust it forever?

Because it describes information at the time it was formed. An edit to a relevant module or reexport relationship could make its answer different. The validator needs to know whether the edited interfaces still support the absence claim.

A cached negative summary can help avoid repeating unrelated work only if changes capable of falsifying it are detectable. Otherwise ‘absent’ is merely the old conclusion, not evidence about the edited program.
What if several wildcard reexports can bring in the same name?

The absence claim must account for every relevant route by which that name could participate in this declaration’s resolution. Validating that one route is unchanged would not establish absence if another route can now contribute a candidate. Likewise, a route becoming nonempty does not by itself determine whether resolution changes; the resulting candidates still have to be assessed under the language’s rules.

The question leaves open how a certificate represents multiple routes. What matters is that none capable of changing the outcome disappears from validation.
Could those paths pass through more than one reexport before reaching a declaration?

If the language permits such a search, the same soundness condition applies through the relevant path: an edit anywhere that can change what reaches the declaration must be able to affect validation of its absence claim. Looking only at the declaration’s immediate import would be insufficient if the effective visible search could change farther away.

That is a conditional design consideration, not an assertion about a particular program, language, or implemented reexport graph.
Do we need to scan all paths if only one imported module was edited?

Not automatically. The aspiration is to distinguish paths the edit could change from paths whose relevant information can be shown unchanged. But a selective check needs a sound basis for ruling a path out. Simply assuming that a path is unaffected because its candidate identities were previously absent would be unsafe.

Whether the design can perform that distinction without examining all paths depends on the available interface information and its change tracking. The question asks how to achieve it; it does not supply a completed answer.
Could we treat a changed import as automatic failure of every absence certificate in that scope?

That would be conservative about some missed additions, but potentially broad. A changed import might not affect a particular name search or trait resolution, so rejecting every certificate in the scope could discard typechecks whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. The aim is to validate the relevant absence claim, rather than equate any import edit with a changed outcome.

Where the validator cannot establish continued absence, it cannot safely accept the certificate. Precision has to be earned by evidence, not by ignoring a possible change.
Is candidate absence the same thing as saying there is no applicable candidate?

Not necessarily. The search might have visible candidates that are inapplicable, while the cached resolution relies on no *additional applicable* candidate changing its outcome. The certificate needs to state the negative fact at a level appropriate to the declaration’s resolution rules. Visibility through wildcard reexports and applicability to the particular use are related but distinct questions.

A design that checks only name presence could overreact to irrelevant additions; one that checks only old applicability facts could miss a newly applicable alternative. The exact certificate claim remains to be defined.
What if the newly visible candidate turns out to be inapplicable?

It may be necessary to reconsider the scoped search to establish that fact. If the candidate cannot affect the declaration’s relevant semantic resolution outcome, the edit need not invalidate the cached typecheck on this dependency alone. Detecting possible impact and deciding that the certificate no longer justifies reuse are distinct steps.

The proposed validation should protect against newly applicable alternatives without treating every new declaration behind a wildcard reexport as a changed typecheck.
Why isn’t the previously selected candidate still being available enough to validate the certificate?

Because candidate absence is about alternatives that might affect the selection. A wildcard reexport can expose a newly applicable candidate while the old selected candidate remains available. A clean build might then choose differently or diagnose ambiguity. Continued availability of the old candidate proves neither continued absence nor unchanged resolution.

The certificate has to validate the negative side of the search as well as any positive fact about the earlier selection.
If the reexport path changes but the final candidate set is identical, does the certificate have to fail?

Not solely because the path changed. A path change makes the earlier absence evidence worth reconsidering; the edited search may still have the same relevant semantic outcome. If validation can establish that the declaration’s required absence and other resolution facts still hold, that edit need not defeat reuse on this ground.

The challenge is providing trustworthy evidence for that conclusion without rescanning every imported module. The question does not say which evidence representation achieves it.
Can one certificate cover several resolution questions in a declaration?

The proposal calls for per-declaration resolution certificates, but that does not imply that validating one absence claim settles all questions the declaration raises. If different overload or trait searches are relevant to its cached typecheck, their required facts must each remain justified. One wildcard-reexport search staying unchanged cannot certify another search that the edit affects.

How multiple claims are packaged is open; the important property is that the certificate cannot hide a changed relevant resolution outcome.
What if an edit changes a wildcard path that previously led to an empty result?

That path still matters if its emptiness helped justify the declaration’s resolution. A negative certificate must keep a route for the edit to trigger validation even when there was no prior candidate identity to record. If the path can now expose a relevant candidate, the old absence claim cannot be accepted without checking the edited search.

Empty results are not dependency-free results.
Does this problem extend to trait implementations found through reexports?

If a language’s trait-implementation visibility or resolution uses the relevant reexport path, then an absence claim for a trait search has the same risk: a candidate not previously participating might become relevant after an edit. The precise visibility and applicability rules are language-dependent, so the certificate must be interpreted according to the search it is actually certifying.

The question is about proving candidate absence across wildcard reexports; it does not establish that every language exposes trait implementations through those paths in the same way.
Would a per-module summary be enough to validate a declaration’s scoped absence?

Only if it can establish what is relevant from the declaration’s scope, including the effects of the applicable wildcard-reexport paths. A summary of a module’s own declarations might omit candidates it reexports, or it might include declarations that are not visible to this use. The validator needs evidence about the effective scoped search, not just an undifferentiated module contents list.

That is a test of a possible summary design, not a claim that per-module summaries are sufficient or insufficient in every language.
If the summary matches its old value, can we avoid rescanning the module?

Potentially, but only if equality soundly means that the module’s contribution to this particular absence claim has not changed, including relevant reexports and visibility. A summary that leaves out a newly participating candidate could match while the clean-build resolution changes. A summary that changes for irrelevant reasons could cause needless checking.

The question is how to make those summaries both complete for the claim and selective enough to avoid blanket rescanning. It supplies no established equality rule.
Is an interface summary alone proof that the final overload resolution is unchanged?

No. An interface summary could help validate candidate absence, but the declaration may also rely on candidate applicability, alias normalization, proof obligations, or coherence-sensitive distinctions. Even within an overload search, a new candidate’s presence does not by itself settle the final selection. The certificate as a whole must justify the relevant semantic outcome before a cached typecheck can be retained.

The current question isolates one particularly difficult part: establishing negative candidate facts through wildcard reexports efficiently.
Could a certificate be valid for an absence claim but still lead to an ambiguity mismatch?

If the ambiguity arises from a candidate or resolution fact outside what the validated absence claim adequately covers, validating that single claim would not justify retaining the whole typecheck. A complete certificate would need to cover all relevant ways an ambiguity could arise for the resolution it certifies.

That is why a validator must not interpret ‘one negative search stayed empty’ as ‘the declaration’s full resolution is unchanged.’ The question does not report such a mismatch; it asks how to prevent one.
How would I tell whether a proposed certificate misses newly exposed candidates?

Ask whether an edit to any wildcard reexport or reachable imported interface that can make a relevant candidate visible will select that declaration’s absence claim for validation. Then ask whether validation of the edited search would recognize the new candidate, including if the earlier search was empty. Finally, ask whether a consequential change leads to reconsideration of the cached declaration.

Those are coverage questions, not an assertion that a particular implementation has been tested or failed.
And how would I judge whether it is selective enough?

Ask whether an edit confined to an unrelated imported module or an unrelated name can be ruled out without rescanning every imported module, and whether a potentially relevant edit that leaves the claim semantically unchanged can be validated without discarding the typecheck unnecessarily. The broader reuse target remains at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged.

Avoiding a scan and retaining a typecheck are different measures. A certificate could retain results but spend substantial work validating them, or avoid work yet reject certificates broadly. This question does not give a performance or reuse result.
What should the validator do when the edited summaries cannot prove that the relevant absence still holds?

It should not use the old absence certificate as sufficient justification for reuse. The affected resolution needs further consideration under the edited program. That may reveal an unchanged outcome, a newly applicable candidate, or an ambiguity; the certificate’s failure to prove absence does not predetermine which.

The conservative fallback protects clean-build parity, while the open design challenge is making validation precise enough that this fallback is not needed for every imported-module edit.
Can we conclude that there is a specific summary structure we should implement?

Not from the question alone. Search-scoped summaries, change tracking for wildcard paths, or other representations can be discussed as possibilities, but none is specified or validated here. The required property is clear: a certificate must soundly establish continued absence of relevant candidates across wildcard reexports using the edited interface information, without demanding a scan of every imported module after each edit.

Any proposed structure would have to be evaluated for both missed changes and unnecessary work.
Can you give me the unresolved question as a precise design criterion?

A per-declaration resolution certificate should remain valid only when edited interface information establishes that every wildcard-reexport route relevant to its scoped candidate search still contributes no candidate that changes the resolution. The design challenge is to locate and check the routes an edit could affect—including previously empty ones—without rescanning every imported module, while allowing results with semantically unchanged resolution dependencies to be reused.

Here’s a hypothesis for wildcard reexports: name-partitioned transitive export summaries with scope-filtered fingerprints should validate wildcard candidate absence without rescanning unrelated modules. How would that work conceptually?

The proposed summary would describe what names can reach a search through transitive exports, rather than requiring the certificate to remember only candidates found previously. Partitioning by name would let validation focus on the name relevant to a particular resolution question. A scope-filtered fingerprint would then represent the part of that name’s export information visible from the declaration’s scope.

If an edit leaves that relevant information semantically unchanged, the certificate’s absence claim could remain justified without scanning unrelated modules. If it can change the claim, the search needs reconsideration. This is the predicted benefit of the hypothesis, not a validated result or a specified summary format.
Why partition by name instead of keeping one summary for all exports?

A change to an unrelated name need not affect an absence claim about the name a declaration is resolving. Name partitioning is intended to keep those changes distinguishable, so validation need not treat every export edit as potentially changing every scoped name search.

The partition still has to reflect the resolver’s actual search rules. Merely giving summaries name labels would not be sufficient if an edit could affect a relevant search without changing the information associated with its name.
What does ‘transitive’ add to the export summary?

It means the summary is intended to account for relevant candidates reachable through chains of exports, including wildcard reexports, not merely declarations directly exported by one module. A certificate claiming absence could be falsified by a candidate introduced farther along a reachable path.

For the hypothesis to hold, an edit anywhere that can alter the effective search for the name must be reflected in the relevant summary. The hypothesis does not specify how that information is propagated.
If the earlier search was empty, what would the certificate actually validate?

It would validate the negative fact that the relevant scoped search still has no candidate that defeats the absence claim. An empty result does not mean there is nothing to track: a later edit could introduce a candidate through a wildcard reexport.

The proposed name-partitioned summary would have to represent that search even when its current answer is empty, and a scope-filtered fingerprint would have to detect a change capable of making that answer relevantly nonempty.
Why filter the fingerprint by scope?

An export can be reachable in some contexts but not visible to the declaration whose certificate is being checked. Scope filtering is meant to make the comparison about the candidate search *from that declaration’s context*, rather than treating every export of the same name as equally relevant.

The filter must be faithful to visibility. If it excludes a candidate that can participate from the declaration’s scope, an unchanged fingerprint could wrongly validate absence. If it includes too much unrelated information, edits may cause needless validation work.
Is a fingerprint itself a proof that no candidate exists?

Not by itself. It can help compare the relevant export information across an edit, but its meaning depends on the summary it fingerprints and whether that summary completely represents the scoped search. A matching value is useful only if it soundly establishes that no consequential change to the absence claim was missed.

The hypothesis proposes using scope-filtered fingerprints for validation; it does not provide their encoding or establish their soundness.
Suppose an unrelated module changes an export with the same name. Would we still have to scan it?

The prediction is that an unrelated module would not have to be rescanned merely because it exports that name. What matters is whether it can contribute to the declaration’s scoped, transitively reachable search. If it cannot, the scope-filtered summary should let validation rule it out.

‘Unrelated’ needs that resolution-based meaning. A module that appears remote in source organization is not unrelated if its exports can reach the declaration through a relevant wildcard path.
What if a reexport path changes but its final contribution for this name stays the same?

The edit may make the summary worth updating or checking, but it need not falsify the certificate’s semantic absence claim. If the edited, scope-filtered summary establishes the same relevant contribution for that name, the path change alone should not require treating the declaration’s resolution as changed.

That is a selectivity the hypothesis aims for. It does not promise that every internal path change can be checked without work.
And what if the path now exposes a new candidate for the name?

A sound transitive summary would have to reflect that newly reachable candidate for scopes from which it is visible. The affected absence claim could no longer be accepted merely on its old evidence; the candidate’s relevance and the edited resolution would have to be assessed.

The new candidate might or might not alter the final resolution. The hypothesis is about making the potentially falsified absence claim discoverable without blanket rescanning, not declaring every newly exposed name an automatic typecheck change.
Could we just compare whether the set of exported names changed?

A name-only set could be too coarse. The same name might remain exported while a different candidate becomes reachable through a wildcard path, or visibility from a particular scope changes. An absence certificate needs information adequate for the candidate search it certifies, not simply a yes-or-no indication that the name occurs somewhere.

The hypothesis calls for *name-partitioned transitive export summaries* and *scope-filtered fingerprints*. Their precise contents remain open, but they must distinguish changes consequential to scoped candidate absence.
Does candidate absence mean no declaration with the name exists anywhere?

No. It concerns the relevant search from a declaration’s scope. A declaration of the same name elsewhere may be invisible or otherwise unable to affect that resolution. The summary and fingerprint are intended to validate that scoped negative fact, not to assert a global absence of the name.
If a new candidate is visible but inapplicable, is the certificate necessarily lost?

The new candidate may require reconsidering the absence claim as it applies to the resolution. Whether it actually defeats the claim depends on what the certificate says—absence of a visible candidate and absence of an applicable alternative are different facts. If validation establishes that the relevant semantic resolution outcome is unchanged, the addition alone need not invalidate the cached typecheck on that basis.

The hypothesis does not specify an applicability test or say that an export fingerprint, by itself, resolves applicability.
Can the summaries handle a wildcard path that previously contributed nothing?

They would need to for this hypothesis to address candidate absence. A previously empty path can later contribute a relevant name, so omitting it from change tracking because it returned nothing would leave a gap. Transitive export information must make that potential contribution visible when the edited interfaces change.

The hypothesis proposes that the summaries can do so; it does not establish a representation for empty paths.
Could a change to visibility alone defeat an absence certificate even if exported candidates are unchanged?

Yes, if it makes an existing candidate visible from the declaration’s scope. That is why scope filtering cannot be treated as an unchanging label attached to a name partition. The fingerprint comparison has to respond to relevant changes in which exported candidates the declaration can see.

Conversely, a visibility edit that leaves this scoped search semantically unchanged need not falsify its absence claim. Both sides matter to the hypothesis.
Does ‘without rescanning unrelated modules’ mean no module is ever revisited after an edit?

No. Relevant summaries may need updating or validation when an edit could change what reaches a scoped search. The predicted saving is avoiding scans of modules that cannot affect the certificate’s claim. It is not a promise that every relevant edit can be handled without examining any interface information.
What is the main soundness risk in relying on a scope-filtered fingerprint?

The risk is treating it as unchanged when a candidate can now reach the declaration through a wildcard reexport. That could happen if the underlying summary omits a transitive route, the scope filter overlooks a visibility change, or the comparison fails to distinguish a consequential change. In that case, the old absence certificate could be accepted despite a different edited search.

Those are conditions to guard against, not reported defects in a particular implementation.
What is the precision risk?

If a fingerprint changes for exports that cannot affect the declaration’s scoped search for this name, validation may revisit or reject certificates unnecessarily. Name partitioning and scope filtering are intended to limit that work and preserve reuse where the resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged.

Precision cannot be obtained by excluding a route that might carry a newly relevant candidate. The proposal needs both accurate coverage and useful discrimination.
Would matching fingerprints be enough to retain the entire declaration typecheck?

No. At most, a sound match would support the particular candidate-absence claim represented by that name-partitioned, scope-filtered summary. The declaration can also depend on positive candidate facts, proof outcomes, alias normalization, coherence, and other typechecking information. Validating one negative fact is not a certificate for the entire result.
What would we have to establish to support the hypothesis?

We would have to show that changes capable of introducing a relevant candidate through any applicable wildcard-reexport path are reflected in the declaration’s name-partitioned, scope-filtered comparison, including when the earlier search was empty. We would also have to show that edits to modules unrelated to that scoped search can be ruled out without rescanning them.

That states what the hypothesis predicts. No implementation, test, or measurement is reported here.
Can you state the hypothesis in one sentence without presenting it as a result?

Name-partitioned transitive export summaries with scope-filtered fingerprints **should** let resolution certificates validate wildcard candidate absence while avoiding rescans of unrelated modules; whether they do so soundly and selectively remains to be established.

Let’s implement name-partitioned export summaries atop DiffResolve v1, then test WildcardExport-400 for clean-build parity and unrelated-module rescans. What are the implementation and evaluation parts of this activity?

The implementation part adds export summaries organized by name to DiffResolve v1. They are intended to help determine whether an edit could change a resolution search through wildcard reexports, including a search that previously found no relevant candidate. The evaluation part runs WildcardExport-400 and checks two things separately: whether incremental results match clean builds, and whether the implementation rescans modules unrelated to the affected search.

This is work to perform and a test to run. It reports neither an implemented summary nor a test result.
What does ‘atop DiffResolve v1’ imply? Are we replacing its resolver updates?

No. DiffResolve v1 is the base into which the name-partitioned export summaries are to be added. The activity does not say to replace its existing differential resolution handling. The summaries address a particular discovery problem: how an edit to exports might affect a candidate search, especially a negative search through wildcard reexports.
Why organize the summaries by name?

A certificate or cached resolution may depend on the absence of a candidate for a particular name. Partitioning export information by name could help distinguish an edit relevant to that search from edits to exports of other names. The intended benefit is to revisit the relevant search without treating every imported module as affected.

That organization must still be sound: a relevant change cannot be omitted merely because no candidate for the name was found before the edit. The activity does not define the summary’s fields or lookup algorithm.
If the old search found no candidate, what is there for the summary to track?

The search itself still matters. A wildcard reexport may provide a route by which a candidate of the relevant name can become visible after an edit. The earlier absence is a fact to revalidate, not a reason to drop the search from consideration.

The proposed summaries need to make a change to that potentially empty contribution discoverable. Otherwise an edit could introduce a relevant candidate without touching any previously recorded candidate identity.
Does a summary of a module’s directly declared names suffice for a wildcard reexport?

Not necessarily. A wildcard reexport can make names reachable through another interface, so validating absence may require accounting for the effective export path, not just direct declarations in one module. An edit along a relevant path could change the name search even while the importing declaration stays untouched.

The implementation task does not prescribe how transitive paths are represented. WildcardExport-400 is the named test for the resulting behavior, not evidence yet that the summaries cover every path.
Should any change to a module exporting the same name force its declarations to be rechecked?

No such blanket rule is specified. An export with the same name might be unrelated to a particular declaration’s visible search. Even a potentially relevant change might leave its semantic resolution outcome unchanged. A summary should help identify searches that warrant reconsideration; a possible effect is not automatically a changed declaration typecheck.

Here’s a hypothesis: SCC-aware, name-partitioned export fixed points with visibility-path witnesses should validate candidate absence across cyclic wildcard reexports without rescanning unrelated modules. How do those pieces fit together?

The proposal treats the effective exports for a particular name as something that may depend on multiple reexport paths, including paths that form cycles. SCC awareness would let the export information for mutually dependent modules be considered consistently. A name partition would keep the question focused on the name relevant to a declaration’s resolution. Visibility-path witnesses would provide checkable evidence about which reexport routes matter from that declaration’s scope.

Together, they are hypothesized to let a certificate validate a negative candidate-search fact after an edit without scanning modules that cannot affect that search. This is a predicted capability, not an established result or a specified implementation.
Why does the hypothesis say ‘export fixed points’ rather than just ‘export summaries’?

A wildcard reexport can depend on another wildcard reexport, which may eventually lead back to the first. In that situation, the effective export information should be mutually consistent; accepting one module’s earlier summary while another relevant summary is being updated could give the wrong answer. The fixed-point framing captures that dependency among export outcomes.

It does not choose an update algorithm or say that every module must be rescanned. It states what the relevant outcomes would need to represent before an absence certificate relies on them.
What work is the SCC awareness doing specifically?

An SCC—a strongly connected component—groups parts of the reexport relationship that can reach one another in a cycle. Recognizing that relationship is intended to prevent an update from stopping at an apparently unchanged export entry when another part of the same cycle can change what is visible through it.

SCC membership alone is not the final answer to a declaration’s name search. The hypothesis still needs the name partition and visibility-path evidence to distinguish which changes could affect that particular search.
If two modules are in one SCC, does any edit to either one invalidate every declaration that imports from the cycle?

No such blanket invalidation is part of the hypothesis. An edit may require updating information within a cyclic export relationship, but a declaration’s relevant candidate absence might remain true. The proposed fixed point should establish the edited export outcome before deciding whether the declaration’s certificate still holds.

Treating every edit within an SCC as a changed declaration outcome would give up the distinction the hypothesis is trying to preserve.
Why partition by name if we already know which reexport cycle changed?

Knowing which cycle is potentially affected need not tell us that every name obtainable through it changed. A name-partitioned outcome would let the compiler consider the particular name a declaration searched for. An edit concerning another name might then leave this absence claim unchanged.

The partition has to be sound under the resolution rules: it cannot exclude a change that could bring a relevant candidate for the searched name into view.
Would one fixed point for each name in each SCC be the required data structure?

That is one way to imagine the combination, but the hypothesis does not prescribe a storage key or a fixed-point algorithm. ‘SCC-aware’ and ‘name-partitioned’ describe properties the export information should have: account for cyclic dependencies and keep relevant names distinguishable. A concrete representation would still have to show that edits reach the right negative searches and that its settled results reflect the edited interfaces.
What is a visibility-path witness supposed to prove when the candidate is absent?

It cannot point to the identity of a candidate that does not exist in the earlier search. Its purpose would be to support a claim about the relevant routes through which a candidate *could* become visible from the declaration’s scope. Validation would need to establish that, under the edited export information, those routes still do not contribute a candidate that defeats the absence claim.

The term ‘witness’ does not specify whether that evidence is stored as paths, summaries, or some other representation. A witness covering only one route would not establish absence if another relevant route remained unchecked.
Does that mean the certificate must enumerate every path through a cycle?

Not necessarily. Cycles can make a literal enumeration of paths a poor way to describe the search. SCC-aware fixed-point information might provide a way to reason about a cyclic group as a whole, while the witness establishes what is relevant to the scoped search. The hypothesis does not decide how that evidence is encoded.

Whatever the representation, it must cover every route that could make a consequential candidate visible. Avoiding explicit enumeration cannot mean silently ignoring a route.
What does ‘cyclic wildcard absence’ mean? Are we claiming no names are exported by the cycle?

No. It is a negative claim about a particular candidate search through cyclic wildcard reexports, from the context of a particular declaration. Other names—or even other candidates for the same name that cannot participate from that context—need not be absent.

The certificate must state its negative fact precisely enough that edited export information can validate it. The hypothesis does not assert that an entire SCC has no exports.
If an edit creates a candidate of the relevant name somewhere in the SCC, must the absence certificate fail?

It must be reconsidered if the new candidate could reach the declaration through a relevant wildcard path. Whether it actually defeats the certified absence depends on the scope and on exactly what absence is being certified. A candidate that cannot be visible from that declaration would not falsify a scoped visibility claim.

Even when a new candidate is visible, determining whether it changes the declaration’s full resolution can require an additional applicability check. Detection of a possible change and a changed final outcome are different conclusions.
Could the path to a candidate change without the exported name changing?

Conceptually, yes. The same name appearing in export information would not, by itself, establish that its visibility from a given declaration is unchanged. A route through wildcard reexports may become available or unavailable from that scope. Visibility-path witnesses are included in the hypothesis so validation concerns the effective scoped search, not just the presence of a name in an undifferentiated export set.

No particular path change is reported by this hypothesis.
What if two different routes expose candidates of the same name?

A certificate of absence must account for all routes that can contribute to the relevant search. A witness supporting one route cannot certify that another contributes nothing consequential. SCC-aware export information would also need to settle how the effective contribution of the cyclic paths is represented before validation relies on it.

The hypothesis does not specify how the language combines candidates exposed by multiple routes or how the witness records them.
How would an edit in a module outside the SCC affect the claim?

Location outside the SCC is not enough to classify the module as unrelated. If its export information can feed a relevant wildcard path into the scoped search, its edit might change the fixed-point outcome or the evidence on which the absence claim rests. If it cannot affect that search, the hypothesis predicts that it can be left out of the rescan work.

‘Unrelated’ is therefore relative to the declaration’s candidate search, not simply to SCC membership or the source-tree layout.
Does ‘without rescanning unrelated modules’ mean that no relevant modules need to be inspected after an edit?

No. An affected export relationship or candidate search may require work to update and validate. The prediction is narrower: information about the relevant name, cyclic dependencies, and visibility paths should let the compiler avoid rescanning modules that cannot affect the certified absence.

The hypothesis does not claim zero validation cost, or give a count of modules that could be skipped.
Could a fingerprint or witness stay the same while the fixed-point outcome changes?

If the recorded evidence were treated as unchanged despite a relevant change to what reaches the declaration, it would not be sound evidence for continued absence. The fixed-point information and visibility-path witness would need to be compared or validated in a way that catches consequential changes through the cycle.

The hypothesis proposes that these pieces can work together; it does not define an equality rule or demonstrate that any particular encoding catches every change.
What if the cycle changes internally but the scoped search remains empty?

Then the edit may require updating the export fixed point and validating the witness, yet the negative fact for this declaration can still hold. On that dependency alone, the cached typecheck need not be discarded merely because the cycle’s internal relationships changed.

That is the precision the hypothesis aims for: distinguish necessary reconsideration of export information from a changed candidate-absence outcome.
Would an unchanged fixed point for the name certify the declaration’s entire typecheck?

No. Even if a sound comparison validates this scoped candidate-absence claim, the declaration may depend on positive candidate information, applicability, trait proofs, alias normalization, coherence, or other typechecking facts. The proposed export mechanism answers a specific negative-search question; it is not a certificate for every part of resolution or the entire typecheck.
What if a newly visible candidate is not applicable to the declaration?

It may change the visible-candidate search while leaving the relevant final resolution outcome unchanged. The validator must be clear about whether its certificate claims absence of *visible* candidates or absence of an *applicable alternative*. Name-partitioned export information and visibility-path evidence can help determine what becomes visible; they do not by themselves establish applicability.

A sound design should detect a potentially consequential new candidate without automatically discarding the declaration’s typecheck when further resolution shows no semantic change.
Does this hypothesis establish that cyclic wildcard searches can always be updated without a full scan?

No. It predicts that the proposed SCC-aware, name-partitioned fixed points and visibility-path witnesses will make it possible to validate cyclic wildcard absence without rescanning *unrelated* modules. Relevant parts of the search may still require examination. Whether the approach actually provides sound coverage and avoids unrelated rescans remains to be established.
What would a correctness check need to catch?

It would need to catch an edit that changes a visibility path through cyclic wildcard reexports so that a candidate can now affect the declaration, including an edited resolution that becomes ambiguous. The incremental diagnostics and applicable executable behavior would have to agree with a clean build of the edited program. Internal agreement of export summaries alone would not establish that observable parity.

This describes how to assess the hypothesis; it does not introduce a test run or claim an outcome.
And what would check the claim about rescanning?

It would distinguish modules whose interface information can affect the scoped name search from modules that cannot, then observe whether validation rescans the latter after edits. A correct clean-build result by itself does not establish that unrelated scans were avoided; a low scan count by itself does not establish that relevant cyclic paths were covered.

No measurement of rescans is included in the hypothesis.
Can you state the failure modes without asserting they’ve happened?

On the soundness side, the fixed-point update might omit a consequential path in a cycle, or a witness might overlook a visibility route from the declaration’s scope. An old absence certificate could then be accepted despite a newly relevant candidate. On the precision side, an edit to a name or module that cannot affect the search might nevertheless cause broad rescanning or needless certificate rejection.

Those are risks a design would have to address, not reported defects of an implementation.
What is the most compact accurate statement of the prediction?

**Hypothesis:** SCC-aware, name-partitioned export fixed points with visibility-path witnesses should validate candidate absence through cyclic wildcard reexports without rescanning unrelated modules. Whether they do so soundly and selectively remains to be tested.

Let’s add SCC-aware export fixed points and visibility-path certificates to DiffResolve v1, then rerun WildcardExport-400 for clean-build parity, rescans, and reuse. What are the implementation and evaluation parts of this activity?

Settling the exports does not, by itself, identify every path relevant to that scoped search; a path certificate is useful only if the export information it relies on reflects the edited program.

Here, SCC awareness concerns *export relationships*: wildcard reexports may form cycles, and effective export information within such a cycle can be mutually dependent. SCC stands for strongly connected component. Recognizing one is a way to reason about a cycle, not a reason to assume every declaration connected to it has changed.

Not merely by establishing visibility. A candidate becoming visible and a candidate being applicable to a particular overload or trait resolution are different questions. Avoiding unnecessary scans must still be justified by sound coverage of the paths that *can* affect the declaration. A low rescan count would not excuse a missed candidate.

Unrelated is relative to the candidate search being checked: its interface information cannot affect the name and visibility paths relevant to that declaration’s resolution. Being in a different module does not suffice, because cross-module reexports can connect the search to it.

The activity does not supply a formal classification procedure or a rescan count. It calls for measuring rescans in the rerun, not assuming in advance which modules will be examined.
